Chapter 1 – Introduction Page 1-1 Chapter 1 Introduction 1.1 Purpose (1) This manual contains the policy, procedures, performance standards and evaluation criteria used by the National Simulator Evaluation Program to evaluate and certify aeroplane and rotorcraft flight simulation training devices (FSTD) pursuant to section 606.03 of the Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs). 1.2 Applicability (1) This manual applies to: (a) Each person using or applying to use an FSTD to meet any requirement of Part IV, Pat VI or Part VII of the CARs; (b) Eligible persons seeking to sponsor an FSTD certification under subsection 606.03(2) of the CARs or pursuant to a Minister approved Bilateral Aviation Safety Agreement between Canada and a foreign state. 1.3 Description of changes (1) Transport Canada Publication (TP) 9685 Revision 3, is a complete reissue that replaces Revision 2. The document has been restructured to eliminate duplication, address new simulator technology and better harmonize with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) standards. The key changes include: (a) The addition of policy to clarify a sponsor’s eligibility and responsibilities when applying for FSTD evaluations and continuing qualification; (b) Alignment of Level 4 to 7 and Level A to D requirements with the qualification performance standards found in FAA Title 14 CFR Part 60; and (c) The introduction of new Level 1 to 2 FSTD standards that are tailored to support Transport Canada training requirements for Private Pilot License (PPL), Commercial Pilot License (CPL), IR and renewal, Multi Crew Coordination (MCC) training as approved by the Minister. 1.4 Reference documents (1) It is intended that the following reference materials be used in conjunction with this document: (a) Aeronautics Act; (b) Part IV, VI and VII of the Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs); (c) Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) 14 CFR Part 60; (d) International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Doc 9625 AN/938 Third Edition 2009 – Manual of Criteria for Qualification of Flight Simulation Training Devices, Volume I (Aeroplanes) and Volume II (Helicopters). 1.5 Definitions and abbreviations (1) The following definitions are used in this document:

Aeroplane and Rotorcraft Simulator Manuel Page 1-2 1st Segment — the portion of the takeoff profile from liftoff to gear retraction. 2nd Segment — the portion of the takeoff profile from after gear retraction to initial flap/slat retraction. 3rd Segment — the portion of the takeoff profile after flap/slat retraction is complete. Aeroplane — a power-driven, heavier-than-air aircraft deriving its lift from aerodynamic reaction from surfaces that remain fixed under given flight conditions. Aircraft — any machine capable of driving support in the atmosphere from reactions of the air. For the purposes of the document, the term includes both aeroplanes and rotorcrafts. Aircraft Data Package — a combination of the various types of data used to design, program, manufacture, modify, and test the FSTD. Airport Models — Class I . Whether modeling real world or fictional airports (or landing areas for helicopters), these airport models (or landing areas for helicopters) are those that meet the requirements of Table A3B or C3B, found in attachment 2 of Appendix A or C, as appropriate, are evaluated by the NSPM, and are listed on the SOQ. Class II . Whether modeling real world or fictional airports (or landing areas for helicopters), these airport models (or landing areas for helicopters) are those models that are in excess of those used for simulator qualification at a specified level. The FSTD sponsor is responsible for determining that these models meet the requirements set out in Table A3C or C3C, found in attachment 2 of Appendix A or C, as appropriate. Class III . This is a special class of airport model (or landing area for helicopters), used for specific purposes, and includes models that may be incomplete or inaccurate when viewed without restriction, but when appropriate limits are applied (e.g., “valid for use only in visibility conditions less than 1⁄2 statute mile or RVR2400 feet,” “valid for use only for approaches to Runway 22L and 22R”), those features that may be incomplete or inaccurate may not be able to be recognized as such by the crewmember being trained, tested, or checked. Class III airport models used for training, testing, or checking activities under this Chapter requires the certificate holder to submit to the TPAA an appropriate analysis of the skills, knowledge, and abilities necessary for competent performance of the task(s) in which this particular model is to be used, and requires TPAA acceptance of each Class III model. Airspeed — calibrated airspeed unless otherwise specified and expressed in terms of nautical miles per hour (knots). Altitude — pressure altitude (meters or feet) unless specified otherwise. Angle of Attack — the angle between the airplane longitudinal axis and the relative wind vector projected onto the airplane plane of symmetry. Approved Check Pilot — means a pilot authorized to conduct Pilot Proficiency Check (PPC) rides on behalf of the Minister. Approved Training Program — means a flight crew member training program approved by the Minister pursuant to the Canadian Aviation Regulations. Automatic Testing — FSTD testing where all stimuli are under computer control. Bank — the airplane attitude with respect to or around the longitudinal axis, or roll angle (degrees). Breakout — the force required at the pilot's primary controls to achieve initial movement of the control position. Certificate Holder — a person issued a certificate under Canadian Aviation Regulation Part IV, VI or VII. Class — in relation to the classification of aeroplanes, means aeroplanes having similar operating characteristics to single-engine aeroplanes, multi-engine aeroplanes, centre-line thrust aeroplanes, land aeroplanes or sea aeroplanes. Closed Loop Testing — a test method where the input stimuli are generated by controllers that drive the FSTD to follow a pre-defined target response. Cockpit — for synthetic flight training device purposes, consists of all that space forward of a cross-section of the fuselage at the most extreme aft setting of the pilot seats. Additional required crew member duty stations and those required bulkheads aft of the pilot seats are also considered part of the cockpit and must replicate the aircraft. Component — means any material, part or sub assembly intended for use on an aeronautical product. Computer Controlled Aircraft — an aircraft where all pilot inputs to the control surfaces are

Aeroplane and Rotorcraft Simulator Manuel Page 1-3 transferred and augmented by computers. Confined Area (helicopter operations) — an area where the flight of the helicopter is limited in some direction by terrain or the presence of natural or man-made obstructions (e.g., a clearing in the woods, a city street, or a road bordered by trees or power lines are regarded as confined areas). Control Sweep — movement of the appropriate pilot controller from neutral to an extreme limit in one direction (Forward, Aft, Right, or Left), a continuous movement back through neutral to the opposite extreme position, and then a return to the neutral position. Convertible FSTD — an FSTD in which hardware and software can be changed so that the FSTD becomes a replica of a different model, usually of the same type aircraft. The same FSTD platform, flight deck shell, motion system, visual system, computers, and peripheral equipment can be used in more than one simulation. Critical Engine Parameter — the parameter that is the most accurate measure of propulsive force. Dead band — the amount of movement of the input for a system for which there is no reaction in the output or state of the system observed. Discrepancy — as used in this part, an aspect of the FSTD that is not correct with respect to the aircraft being simulated. This includes missing, malfunctioning, or inoperative components that are required to be present and operate correctly for training, evaluation, and experience functions to be creditable. It also includes errors in compliance processes or the documentation used to support the FSTD (e.g. MQTG errors, information missing from the MQTG, or required statements from appropriately qualified personnel). Distance — the length of space between two points, expressed in terms of nautical miles unless otherwise specified. Downgrade — a permanent change in the qualification level of an FSTD to a lower level. Driven — a test method where the input stimulus or variable is positioned by automatic means, usually a computer input. Electronic Copy of the MQTG — an electronic copy of the MQTG provided by an electronic scan presented in a format, acceptable to the NSPM. Electronic Master Qualification Test Guide — an electronic version of the MQTG (eMQTG), where all objective data obtained from airplane testing, or another approved source, together with correlating objective test results obtained from the performance of the FSTD and a description of the equipment necessary to perform the evaluation for the initial and the recurrent evaluations is stored, archived, or presented in either reformatted or digitized electronic format. End-to-End Testing — is the process in which control displacements are used as inputs. Engine — as used in this part, the appliance or structure that supplies propulsive force for movement of the aircraft: i.e., the turbine engine for turbine powered aircraft; the turbine engine and propeller assembly for turbo-propeller powered aircraft; and the reciprocating engine and propeller assembly for reciprocating engine powered aircraft. For purposes of this part, engine failure is the failure of either the engine or propeller assembly to provide thrust higher than idle power thrust due to a failure of either the engine or the propeller assembly. Evaluation —With respect to an FSTD, the qualification activities for the device (e.g., the objective and subjective tests, the inspections, or the recurrent evaluations) associated with the requirements of this manual. Fictional Airport — a visual model of an airport that is a collection of “non-real world” terrain, instrument approach procedures, navigation aids, maps, and visual modeling detail sufficient to enable completion of an Airline Transport Pilot Certificate or Type Rating. Flight Crew Member — means a pilot or flight engineer assigned to duties in an aircraft during flight time. Flight Simulation Training Device (FSTD) — means an apparatus, including synthetic flight training equipment that replicates or emulates an aircraft or aircraft component for the purpose of pilot training and checking. The term refers to both a full flight simulator (FFS) and a flight training device (FTD). Flight Test Data — (a subset of objective data) aircraft data collected by the aircraft manufacturer or other acceptable data supplier during an aircraft flight test program. Flight Training Device (FTD) — a replica of aircraft instruments, equipment, panels, and controls in an open flight deck area or an enclosed aircraft flight deck replica. It includes the equipment and computer programs necessary to represent aircraft (or set of aircraft) operations in ground and flight

Aeroplane and Rotorcraft Simulator Manuel Page 1-4 conditions having the full range of capabilities of the systems installed in the device as described in the qualification performance standard (QPS) for a specific FTD qualification level. Free Response — the response of the FSTD after completion of a control input or disturbance. Frozen — a test condition where one or more variables are held constant with time. FSTD Approval — the extent to which an FSTD may be used by a certificate holder as authorized by the FAA. FSTD Directive — a document issued by the Transport Canada to an FSTD sponsor requiring a modification to the FSTD due to a safety-of-flight issue and amending the qualification basis for the FSTD. FSTD Latency — the additional time for the FSTD to respond to input that is beyond the response time of the aircraft. FSTD Performance — the overall performance of the FSTD, including aircraft performance (e.g., thrust/drag relationships, climb, range) and flight and ground handling. Full Flight Simulator (FFS) — a replica of a specific type, make, model, or series aircraft. It includes the equipment and computer programs necessary to represent aircraft operations in ground and flight conditions, a visual system providing an out-of-the-flight deck view, a system that provides cues at least equivalent to those of a three-degree-of-freedom motion system, and has the full range of capabilities of the systems installed in the device as described the QPS for a specific FFS qualification level. Functional Checks — means subjective checks carried out on an FSTD by a pilot qualified on the aircraft type supported by the device, to confirm that the FSTD handles like the aircraft to the extent that a pilot can accomplish all critical training and checking sequences and manoeuvres for which the device is intended to be credited. Gate Clutter — the static and moving ground traffic (e.g., other airplanes; tugs; power or baggage carts; fueling, catering, or cargo trucks; pedestrians) presented to pose a potential conflict with the simulated aircraft during ground operations around the point where the simulated airplane is to be parked between flights Generic Airport Model — a Class III visual model that combines correct navigation aids for a real world airport with a visual model that does not depict that same airport. Grandfathering — as used in this manual, the practice of assigning a qualification basis for an FSTD based on the period of time during which a published set of standards governed the requirements for the initial and continuing qualification of FSTDs. Each FSTD manufactured during this specified period of time is “grandfathered” or held to the standards that were in effect during that time period. The grandfathered standards remain applicable to each FSTD manufactured during the stated time period regardless of any subsequent modification to those standards and regardless of the sponsor, as long as the FSTD remains qualified or is maintained in a non-qualified status in accordance with the specific requirements and time periods prescribed in this manual. Gross Weight — for objective test purposes: Basic Operating Weight (BOW) — the empty weight of the aircraft plus the weight of the following: Normal oil quantity; lavatory servicing fluid; potable water; required crewmembers and their baggage; and emergency equipment. Light Gross Weight — a weight chosen by the sponsor or data provider that is not more than 120% of the BOW of the aircraft being simulated or the minimum practical operating weight of the test aircraft. Medium Gross Weight — a weight chosen by the sponsor or data provider that is within 10% of the average of the numerical values of the BOW and the maximum certificated gross weight. Near Maximum Gross Weight — a weight chosen by the sponsor or data provider that is not less than the BOW of the aircraft being simulated plus 80% of the difference between the maximum certificated gross weight (either takeoff weight or landing weight, as appropriate for the test) and the BOW. Ground Effect — the change in aerodynamic characteristics due to of the change in the airflow past the aircraft caused by the proximity of the earth's surface to the airplane. Hands Off — a test maneuver conducted without pilot control inputs. Hands On — a test maneuver conducted with pilot control inputs as required. Heave — FSTD movement with respect to or along the vertical axis. Height — the height above ground level (or AGL) expressed in meters or feet. “ In Use” Runway — as used in this part, the runway that is currently selected, able to be used for

Aeroplane and Rotorcraft Simulator Manuel Page 1-5 takeoffs and landings, and has the surface lighting and markings required by this part. Also known as the “active” runway. Integrated Testing — testing of the FSTD so that all aircraft system models are active and contribute appropriately to the results. With integrated testing, none of the models used are substituted with models or other algorithms intended for testing only. Irreversible Control System — a control system where movement of the control surface will not back-drive the pilot's control on the flight deck. Latency — means the additional time beyond that of the basic aircraft perceivable response time due to the response of the simulator. This includes the update rate of the host computer added to the respective time delays of the motion system, visual system or instruments. Line Oriented Flight Training (LOFT) — means a training and checking program approved by the Minister pursuant to the Canadian Aviation Regulations which uses an approved simulator capable of representing the air operator's route structure and which incorporates realistic pre flight briefings, communications procedures and normal, abnormal and emergency procedures. Locked — a test condition where one or more variables are held constant with time. Management Representative — an employee of the sponsor delegated with the responsibility and authority to monitor the on-going qualification of assigned FSTDs and liaise with Transport Canada National Simulator Evaluation Program (NSEP) on the sponsor’s behalf. Manager, Simulator Program (MSP) — the Transport Canada manager responsible for the overall administration and direction of the NSEP or a person approved by that Transport Canada manager. Manual Testing — FSTD testing conducted without computer inputs except for initial setup, and all modules of the simulation are active. Master Qualification Test Guide (MQTG) — the Transport Canada-approved Qualification Test Guide with the addition of the Transport Canada-witnessed test results, applicable to each individual FSTD. Medium — the normal operational weight for a given flight segment. Minister — means the Minister of Transport. Near Limiting Performance — the performance level the operating engine must be required to achieve to have sufficient power to land a helicopter after experiencing a single engine failure during takeoff of a multiengine helicopter. The operating engine must be required to operate within at least 5 percent of the maximum RPM or temperature limits of the gas turbine or power turbine, or operate within at least 5 percent of the maximum drive train torque limits. Near limiting performance is based on the existing combination of density altitude, temperature, and helicopter gross weight. Nominal — the normal operating configuration, atmospheric conditions, and flight parameters for the specified flight segment. Non-Normal Control — a term used in reference to Computer Controlled Aircraft. It is the state where one or more of the intended control, augmentation, or protection functions are not fully working. Note: Specific terms such as ALTERNATE, DIRECT, SECONDARY, or BACKUP may be used to define an actual level of degradation. Normal Control — a term used in reference to Computer Controlled Aircraft. It is the state where the intended control, augmentation, and protection functions are fully working. Objective Data — quantitative data, acceptable to the NSPM, used to evaluate the FSTD. Objective Test — a quantitative measurement and evaluation of FSTD performance. Operator — A certificate holder using an FSTD pursuant to CAR requirements. Pitch — the airplane attitude with respect to, or around, the lateral axis expressed in degrees. Power Lever Angle (PLA) — the angle of the pilot's primary engine control lever(s) on the flight deck. This may also be referred to as THROTTLE or POWER LEVER. Predicted Data — estimations or extrapolations of existing flight test data or data from other simulation models using engineering analyses, engineering simulations, design data, or wind tunnel data. Protection Functions — systems functions designed to protect an airplane from exceeding its flight maneuver limitations. Pulse Input — a step input to a control followed by an immediate return to the initial position. Qualification Level — the categorization of an FSTD established by the MSP based on the FSTDs demonstrated technical and operational capabilities as prescribed in this document. Qualification Performance Standard (QPS) — the collection of procedures and criteria used when conducting objective and subjective tests, to establish FSTD qualification levels. The QPS are

Aeroplane and Rotorcraft Simulator Manuel Page 1-6 published in the appendices Chapters 4,5 and 6. Qualification Test Guide (QTG) — the primary reference document used for evaluating an aircraft FSTD. It contains test results, statements of compliance and capability, validation data, the configuration of the aircraft simulated, and other information for the simulator evaluation specialist to assess the FSTD against the applicable regulatory criteria. Quality Management System (QMS) — a flight simulation quality-systems that can be used for external quality-assurance purposes. It is designed to identify the processes needed, determine the sequence and interaction of the processes, determine criteria and methods required to ensure the effective operation and control of the processes, ensure the availability of information necessary to support the operation and monitoring of the processes, measure, monitor, and analyze the processes, and implement the actions necessary to achieve planned results. Real-World Airport — as used in this part in reference to airport visual models, a computer generated visual depiction of an existing airport. Representative — when used as an adjective in this part, typical, demonstrative, or characteristic of, the feature being described. For example, “representative sampling of tests” means a sub-set of the complete set of all tests such that the sample includes one or more of the tests in each of the major categories, the results of which provide the evaluator with an overall understanding of the performance and handling characteristics of the FSTD. Reversible Control System — a control system in which movement of the control surface will back-drive the pilot's control on the flight deck. Roll — the airplane attitude with respect to, or around, the longitudinal axis expressed in degrees. Rotorcraft — means a power driven, heavier than air aircraft supported in flight by the reaction of air on one or more rotors. Set of Aircraft — a group or series of aircraft that share similar handling and operating characteristics, similar operating envelopes, and have the same number and type of engines or power-plants. Sideslip Angle — the angle between the relative wind vector and the airplane plane of symmetry. (Note: this definition replaces the current definition of “sideslip.”) Similar Type Aeroplane — means an aeroplane in the same propulsion category. The propulsion categories are turbo-jet, turbo-propeller or reciprocating. Simulation Quality Management System (SQMS) — the elements of a quality management system for FSTD continuing qualification. Simulator Evaluation Specialist — is a Transport Canada technical specialist, trained to evaluate simulators and to provide expertise on matters concerning aircraft simulation. Small aircraft — means an aeroplane having a maximum permissible take-off weight of 5 700 kg (12,566 pounds) or less, or a helicopter having a maximum permissible take-off weight of 2 730 kg (6,018 pounds) or less. Snapshot — means a presentation of one or more variables at a given instant of time. A snapshot is associated with a steady state condition in which the variables are essentially constant over time. Special Evaluation — an evaluation of the FSTD for purposes other than initial, upgrade, or continuing qualification. Circumstances that may require a special evaluation include movement of the FSTD to a different location, or an update to FSTD software or hardware that might affect performance or flying qualities Sponsor — a certificate holder under CAR Part IV, VI or VII, who seeks to operate an FSTD under CAR 606.03 and is responsible for requesting and maintaining an FSTD qualification in accordance with the requirements of and applicable Qualification Performance Standards (QPS) in this manual. Statement of Compliance and Capability (SOC) — a declaration that a specific requirement has been met and explaining how the requirement was met (e.g., gear modeling approach, coefficient of friction sources). The SOC must also describe the capability of the FSTD to meet the requirement, including references to sources of information for showing compliance, rationale to explain how the referenced material is used, mathematical equations and parameter values used, and conclusions reached. Step Input — an abrupt control input held at a constant value. Subjective Test — a qualitative assessment of the performance and operation of the FSTD. Surge — FSTD movement with respect to or along the longitudinal axis. Sway — FSTD movement with respect to or along the lateral axis. Synthetic Flight Training Device — Is the Canadian Aviation Regulation definition of an aircraft

Aeroplane and Rotorcraft Simulator Manuel Page 1-7 full flight simulator or a flight training device that meets the standards set out in this manual for the purpose of permitting experience acquired therein to be credited towards meeting the requirements for a pilot proficiency check, the issue of a flight crew license, or the endorsement of a rating. [For the purposes of this document, the ICAO term “Flight Simulation Training Device” (FSTD) is used in lieu of Synthetic Flight Training Device]. Time History — a presentation of the change of a variable with respect to time. Ti — Total time from initial throttle movement until a 10% response of a critical engine parameter. Tf — Total time of the flare maneuver. Tt — Total time from initial throttle movement to an increase of 90% of go around power or a decrease of 90% from maximum take-off power. Training Program Approval Authority (TPAA) — For the purposes of this manual, the Training Program Approving Authority (TPAA) means the person in Transport Canada delegated by the Minister to approve a certificate holder’s pilot training and checking program, and authorize the use of a particular FSTD in that approved training program. Training Restriction — a temporary condition where an FSTD with missing, malfunctioning, or inoperative (MMI) components may continue to be used at the qualification level indicated on its SOQ, but restricted from completing the tasks for which the correct function of the MMI component is required. Transport Delay or “Throughput ” — the total FSTD system processing time required for an input signal from a pilot primary flight control until motion system, visual system, or instrument response. It is the overall time delay incurred from signal input to output response. It does not include the characteristic delay of the airplane simulated. Update — an improvement to or modernization of the quality or the accuracy of the FSTD without affecting the qualification level of the FSTD. Upgrade — the improvement or enhancement of an FSTD for the purpose of achieving a higher qualification level. Validation Data — objective data used to determine if the FSTD performance is within the tolerances prescribed in the QPS. Validation Test — an objective test where FSTD parameters are compared to the relevant validation data to ensure that the FSTD performance is within the tolerances prescribed in the QPS. Visual Data Base — a display that may include one or more airport models. Visual System Response Time — the interval from a control input to the completion of the visual display scan of the first video field containing the resulting different information. Yaw — the airplane attitude with respect to, or around, the vertical axis expressed in degrees.

Chapter 2 – Policies and Procedures Page 2-1 Chapter 2 Policies and Procedures 2.1 Flight Simulation Training Device Use (1) Pursuant to section 606.03 of the Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), no person may use an Flight Simulation Training Device (FSTD) for pilot training or a pilot proficiency check required under Part IV, Part VI, or Part VII of the CARs unless the FSTD operator (sponsor) holds a FSTD certificate issued by the Minister. The Manager, Simulator Program (MSP) will issue a certificate on behalf of the Minister upon determining whether the FSTD: (a) Satisfies the applicable qualification performance standard for the level of qualification requested; and (b) Has a single FSTD sponsor who is eligible under section 2.6 of this manual. The sponsor may arrange with another person for services of document preparation and presentation, as well as FSTD inspection, maintenance, repair, and servicing; however, the sponsor remains responsible for ensuring that these functions are conducted in a manner and with a result of continually meeting the requirements of this manual. (c) Remains qualified as described in the FSTD Qualification Certificate issued to the sponsor, through satisfactory inspection, recurrent evaluations, appropriate maintenance, and use in accordance with the applicable Qualification Performance Standards (QPS) and requirements in this manual. (d) Functions during day-to-day pilot training and checking activities with the software and hardware that was evaluated as satisfactory by the National Simulator Evaluation Program (NSEP) and, any modifications are implemented in accordance with the requirements at paragraph 2.16. (e) Is operated in accordance with the provisions and limitations of section 2.10. Note : A person who knowingly makes any false representation for the purpose of obtaining a FSTD qualification certificate or any privilege accorded thereby; or makes or causes to be made any false entry in a record required under this manual with intent to mislead or willfully omit to make any entry in any such record may be subject to action under Part 7.3 (1) of the Aeronautics Act . (f) Once the Minister has issues an FSTD certificate to a sponsor, that FSTD is eligible for use by any Canadian Air Operator or Private Operator provided that they each receive approval from their Training Program Approval Authority (TPAA) to use the device in their respective approved training or checking program. 2.2 Manager of Simulator Program Responsibilities (1) The Manager of the MSP is the Minister’s delegate responsible for assigning FSTD evaluations and issuing certificates required by section 606.03 of the CARs except in those cases where oversight of a non-type-specific FTD is delegated to Regional Authority (Chapter 6). (2) Before issuing an initial FSTD qualification certificate to the sponsor, the MSP or Regional Authority shall review the initial evaluation report to verify compliance and ensure the sponsor satisfies the eligibility criteria. (3) Unless it is otherwise deemed in the interest of the Minister, the MSP will only accept requests for evaluations if:

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-2 (a) The applicant or sponsor is eligible as per section 2.6; and (b) The FSTD is intended for use in a Transport Canada approved training program; or if it is used by an operator holding a Transport Canada Air Operator or Private Operator Certificate in the course of conducting Pilot Proficiency Checks (PPC) or for the issuance of flight crew licences or a type rating endorsement. (4) The MSP may remove some or all of an FSTD qualification including the withdrawal of approval to use an FSTD in a Transport Canada approved training program; or deny an application for a qualification for reasons identified at section 2.11 of this Chapter. 2.3 Training Program Approval Authority Responsibilities (1) For the purposes of this manual, the Training Program Approving Authority (TPAA) means the person in Transport Canada delegated by the Minister to approve a certificate holder’s pilot training and checking program, and who authorizes the use of a particular FSTD in that approved training program. (2) The TPAA is responsible for: (a) Approving the use of a certified FSTD in the sponsor’s Transport Canada approved training program; (b) Determining whether a specific FSTD, or combination of FSTDs / aircraft are required to satisfy all elements in the sponsor’s Transport Canada approved training program; (c) Approving short term changes to an approved training program or session to accommodate a malfunctioning, or inoperative (MMI) declared under the provisions of section 2.10. Note: In accordance with paragraph 2.7 (4) , for each Canadian Air Operator or Private Operator using the FSTD, the sponsors must keep a copy of the TPAA’s written approval to use the FSTD in their respective Transport Canada approved training program. 2.4 Evaluation Types (1) The National Simulator Evaluation Program conducts the following types of evaluations for the certification and continuing qualification of FSTDs pursuant to section 606.03 of the CARs. Application instructions and procedures for eligible sponsors and applicants are found at Chapter 3: (a) Initial Evaluation : An evaluation for the purpose of determining the qualification level of an FSTD and assessing the sponsor’s procedures and processes required to maintain compliance with this document. (b) Recurrent Evaluation : A periodic evaluation of an FSTD to confirm the continuing qualification of the FSTD and compliance with sponsor requirements herein. This evaluation consists of objective tests, subjective tests, and verification that FSTD and sponsor continue to meet general requirements, as described in the applicable QPS as may be amended. Note: The frequency of recurrent evaluations for Full Flight Simulators (FFS) and Flight Training Devices (FTD) are established by subsection 606.03 (5) of the CARs. (c) Foreign Evaluation: An initial or recurrent evaluation of an FSTD located outside of Canada for an eligible applicant and FSTD sponsor. (d) Upgrade Evaluation: An initial evaluation of a previously qualified FSTD for the purpose of raising its qualification level.

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-3 (e) Update Evaluation: A focused evaluation to verify the performance and functionality of a modification, improvement, or change to the FSTD that impacts the qualification performance as described in the MQTG, or changes the qualifications identified on the Qualification Certificate. (f) Special Evaluation: An evaluation conducted at the discretion of the MSP to restore the qualification of an FSTD after a voluntary suspension, sponsor change, FSTD relocation, or qualification suspension / downgrade imposed due to unsatisfactory FSTD condition, performance or compliance to sponsor requirements. The scope of the evaluation will be determined by the MSP on a case-by-case basis. 2.5 Qualification Performance Standards (1) The Qualification Performance Standards (QPS) are a collection of procedures and criteria used when conducting objective and subjective tests, to evaluate and establish an FSTD qualification level. The QPS are published in appendices to this manual as follows: (a) Chapter 4 - QPS for full flight simulators (FFS): (i) Appendix A - aeroplane FFS (Level A, B, C, D); (ii) Appendix B - rotorcraft FFS (Level B, C, D). (b) Chapter 5 - QPS for type-specific flight training devices (FTD): (i) Appendix C - aeroplane FTD (Level 4, 5, 6, 7); (ii) Appendix D - rotorcraft FTD (level 4, 5, 6, 7); and (c) Chapter 6 - QPS for non-type-specific flight training devices: (i) Appendix E - aeroplane FTD (Level 1 and 2); and (ii) Appendix F - rotorcraft FTD (Level 1 and 2). Note: Level 3 FTD QPS reserved for potential growth of non-type-specific FTD credits and therefore not published in this document. (2) Initial Evaluations - After the effective date of this manual, initial evaluations shall be conducted using the qualification performance standards of this manual except where the Minister has accepted: (a) An earlier standard for previously qualified or relocated simulator that satisfies the conditions at paragraphs (2.5 (3) , 2.5 (5) , or 2.5 (6) ; or (b) An earlier standard for FTSDs located in a foreign state that is currently qualified by the foreign state authority and satisfies the conditions at paragraph 2.5 (7) . (3) FSTDs Previously Qualified . FSTDs with a valid Transport Canada NSEP qualification prior to the effective date of this manual will continue to be qualified based on the standard and criteria used when it was initially evaluated or last upgraded provided that: (a) It continues to meet the standards, including the objective test results recorded in the MQTG and subjective tests, under which it was originally evaluated, regardless of sponsor; (b) The sponsor complies with the other applicable provisions herein; and (c) Any change in FSTD qualification level initiated is re-evaluated in accordance with the applicable QPS herein. Note: For previously qualified FSTDs, the conditions for restoring a qualification that has been automatically lost or withdrawn are described at paragraph 2.13 (2) .

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-4 (4) Request for Qualification Downgrade . A sponsor may request that an FSTD be permanently downgraded. In such a case, the MSP may downgrade a qualified FSTD without requiring and without conducting an initial evaluation for the new qualification level. Subsequent recurrent evaluations will use the existing MQTG, modified as necessary to reflect the new qualification level. When the sponsor has appropriate validation data available and receives approval from the MSP, the sponsor may adopt tests and associated tolerances described in this manual as the basis for continuing qualification of a previously qualified FSTD. The updated test(s) and tolerance(s) must be included as a permanent part of the MQTG. (5) Sponsor change or FSTDs Relocated within Canada – An FSTD relocated within Canada or undergoing a sponsorship change will require a special evaluation. The MSP will determine the scope of the evaluation on a case-by-case basis. The evaluation may be based on the standard used when the FSTD was first qualified or last upgraded provided that it was operating in compliance with that standard within one calendar year of the special evaluation to re-instate the qualification. FSTDs not meeting this condition or having undergone significant updates in conjunction with the relocation will be subject to an initial evaluation based on the standards and criteria herein. (6) FSTDs Relocated to Canada – FSTDs relocated to Canada from another country will require an initial evaluation. The MSP may accept the following qualification performance standards for initial evaluations of Level 4 to 7 and Level A to D FSTDs provided that the FSTD was operating in compliance with that standard within one calendar year of the initial evaluation. The sponsor must continue to comply with all other procedures and policies herein: (a) FAA Title 14 CFR Part 60 as amended; (b) EASA CS-FSTD(A) as amended; (c) EASA CS-FSTD(H) as amended; (d) FAA AC 120-40C for simulators built before 01 January 2009; (e) JAR FSTD A for simulators built before 08 April 2012; or (f) JAR-STD 1A as amended for simulators built before 08 April 2012. (7) Foreign Initial Evaluations – In addition to the QPS in this manual, the MSP may accept the following standards for initial evaluations conducted on FSTDs located outside Canada provided that the simulator sponsor holds a current simulator qualification to that standard from EASA or the FAA. The sponsor must continue to comply with all other procedures and policies herein: (a) FAA AC 120-40B for simulators built before 01 January 1998; or (b) FAA AC 120-40C for simulators built before 01 January 2009; or (c) JAR FSTD A for simulators built before 08 April 2012; or (d) JAR-STD 1A as amended for simulators built before 08 April 2012. 2.6 Sponsor Eligibility (1) Within Canada: A person is eligible to apply to be a sponsor of an FSTD located in Canada if the following conditions are met: (a) The person holds, or is an applicant for, a Private Operator Certificate under Part VI of the CARs, an Air Operator Certificate under Part VII of the CARs, or a Flight Training Unit or Approved Training Organization (ATO) Certificate under Part IV of the CARs; and (b) The FSTD will be used, or will be offered for use, in the sponsor’s Transport Canada approved flight training program for the aircraft being simulated as evidenced in a request for evaluation submitted to the NSEP.

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-5 (2) Outside of Canada: Application for initial or recurrent evaluations of FSTDs located outside Canada must originate from a Canadian Air Operator holding a certificate under Part VII of the CARs or a Canadian Private Operator holding a certificate under Part VI of the CARs provided that: (a) The (foreign) FSTD sponsor holds a certificate under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) part 119, 141, or 142; or an EASA certificate for an Approved Training Organization (ATO), or a Type Rating Training Organization (TRTO); and (b) The specific aircraft or set of aircraft simulated has a Transport Canada type-certificate authorizing their operation in Canada, and (c) The TPAA approves the use of the FSTD in the applicant’s Transport Canada approved training program; and (d) The applicant signs an agreement for recovering the incremental costs of providing services outside of Canada (form 26-0622 (0710-03). Note: The MSP may accept the evaluation and qualification of an FSTD located in a foreign state if there is a Bilateral Aviation Safety Agreement and Simulator Implementation Plan between Canada and that foreign state. See Chapter 3, Section 3.9 for application procedures and requirements. 2.7 Additional Responsibilities of the Sponsor (1) Upon request, the sponsor must allow the NSEP to inspect the FSTD as soon as practicable. This inspection may include all records and documents relating to the FSTD compliance with the requirements herein. (2) For each FSTD, the sponsor must post in or adjacent to the FSTD the Qualification Certificate issued by Transport Canada NSEP. An electronic copy of the Qualification Certificate that may be accessed via an appropriate terminal or display in or adjacent to the FSTD is satisfactory. (3) Each sponsor of an FSTD must identify to the MSP by name, one individual to be the management representative (MR). (a) One person may serve as an MR for more than one FSTD, but one FSTD must not be represented by more than one person serving in this capacity. (b) Each MR must be an employee of the sponsor with the responsibility and authority to monitor the on-going qualification of assigned FSTDs to ensure that all matters regarding FSTD qualification are being carried out in accordance with the provisions herein.; (c) The MR serves as the primary contact point for all matters between the sponsor and the NSEP regarding the qualification of that FSTD in accordance with the provisions herein. (4) Sponsors holding a Transport Canada NSEP Qualification Certificate for an FSTD located outside of Canada are responsible for ensuring that each Canadian Air Operator or Private Operator using the FSTD provides written approval from their TPAA. The sponsor must keep this approval on file and produce it to the MSP upon request. (5) For each Transport Canada qualified FFS and Level 4, 5, 6, and 7 FTD, the sponsor must obtain a written statement at least annually from a qualified pilot who has flown the aircraft or set of aircraft (as appropriate) during the preceding 12-month period stating that the subject FSTD’s performance and handling qualities, within the normal operating envelope, represent the aircraft or set of aircraft described in the Transport Canada Type Certificate and the type data sheet, if appropriate. The sponsor must retain the two most current written statements for review by the MSP. (6) Special equipment and personnel requirements for qualification of the FSTD . When notified by the MSP, the sponsor must make available all special equipment and qualified personnel

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-6 needed to accomplish or assist in the accomplishment of tests during initial qualification, continuing qualification, or special evaluations. (7) The sponsor is responsible for ensuring that recurrent evaluations are scheduled and confirmed with the NSEP no later than 60 days before the evaluation is due. 2.8 Compliance Processes (1) The sponsor must establish effective processes and auditable documentation to maintain continuing qualification of an FSTD in accordance with the applicable QPS, and to ensure compliance with sponsor requirements. Compliance processes will include procedures, methods and mechanisms to: (a) Accomplish all appropriate objective tests each year as specified in the applicable QPS and ensuring the test results are reviewed by a qualified person. (b) Complete a functional pre-flight check on each FSTD within the preceding 24 hours. (c) Provide the MSP access to the objective test results in the MQTG and access to the FSTD for the length of time necessary for the MSP to complete the required recurrent evaluations. (d) Maintain a process for corrective and preventive maintenance on the FSTD to ensure that it continues to meet the requirements of the applicable QPS appendix. The process will be supported by a discrepancy log that ensures, when a discrepancy is discovered, the following requirements are met: (i) A description of each discrepancy is entered in the log and remains in the log until the discrepancy is corrected. (ii) A description of the corrective action taken for each discrepancy, the identity of the individual taking the action, and the date that action is taken is entered in the log. (iii) The discrepancy log is kept in a form and manner acceptable to the Minister and is kept in or adjacent to the FSTD. An electronic log that may be accessed by an appropriate terminal or display in or adjacent to the FSTD is satisfactory. (2) Maintain revision control of the MQTG; (3) Maintain a current list of missing, malfunctioning or inoperative components in accordance with paragraph 2.10 (2) . (4) Notify the MSP in writing of intentions to modify the FSTD; (5) Notify the MSP when a modification has been completed and verified by a qualified pilot and technician to meet the functional, subjective and objective tests requirements of the applicable QPS; (6) Maintain records in plain language form or in coded form if the coded form provides for the preservation and retrieval of information in a manner acceptable to the MSP of: (a) Results of the qualification evaluations (initial and each upgrade) since the issuance of the original Qualification Certificate, and (b) Results of the objective tests conducted in accordance with paragraph 2.8 (1) (a) for a period of 2 years, and (c) The MQTG and each amendment thereto, and (d) A record of all FSTD modifications affected under paragraph 2.16 since the issuance of the original Qualification Certificate, and

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-7 (e) Results of the previous three recurrent evaluations, or the recurrent evaluations from the previous 2 years, whichever covers a longer period, and (f) A complete record of all discrepancies entered in the discrepancy log over the previous 2 years. Note: A person who knowingly makes any false representation for the purpose of obtaining a FSTD qualification certificate or any privilege accorded thereby; or makes or causes to be made any false entry in a record required under this manual with intent to mislead or wilfully omit to make any entry in any such record may be subject to action under Part 7.3 (1) of the Aeronautics Act. 2.9 FSTD Performance Degradation and Discrepancy Reporting (1) Logging FSTD discrepancies. Each instructor, or delegate of the Minister conducting pilot training or pilot proficiency checks pursuant to CAR requirements, and each person conducting the pre-flight inspection who discovers a discrepancy, including any missing, malfunctioning, or inoperative components in the FSTD, must write or cause to be written a description of that discrepancy into the discrepancy log at the end of the FSTD pre-flight or FSTD use session. (2) If the performance of an FSTD does not accurately simulate the flight characteristics of the aircraft or if special techniques not in common with the aeroplane are necessary to control the FSTD, the Inspector or Approved Check Pilot (ACP) is to terminate the check. (a) If the FSTD is located in Canada, he/she will enter in the discrepancy log the statement “unsuitable for the conduct of a Pilot Proficiency Check (PPC)” along with sufficient substantiating details. If the FSTD can be returned to service without changes to its program, the signature of an Inspector qualified on type may authorize reinstatement of training and checking privileges. Should changes in the simulator programming be required, re-approval of the simulator will require authorization by the MSP. (b) If it is necessary to terminate or restrict a check utilizing a simulator located outside of Canada, he/she will inform the representative of the Canadian operator using the FSTD that it is not suitable for a PPC and notify the MSP. The entry in the discrepancy log will not include the statement “unsuitable for the conduct of a Pilot Proficiency Check (PPC)”. (3) If a simulator’s motion system, flight control system, or a system / component necessary for the FSTD occupants’ safety is inoperative or malfunctioning, the simulator must be declared “unsuitable for Pilot Training or Checking”. The MSP must be notified and appropriate entries must be made in the simulator discrepancy log. 2.10 Simulator Component Inoperative Guide and Operation with missing, malfunctioning, or inoperative components. (1) For the purposes of this document, a missing, malfunctioning, or inoperative (MMI) component pertains to any FSTD component, hardware / software appliance or function that is required to be present and correctly operate for the satisfactory completion of a maneuver, procedure, or task that is necessary to meet an element in an approved training or checking program. (2) The Sponsor is responsible for: (a) Maintaining a current list of the MMI components that is readily available in or adjacent to the FSTD for review by users of the device. Electronic access to this list via an appropriate terminal or display in or adjacent to the FSTD is satisfactory. The discrepancy log may be used to satisfy this requirement provided each currently MMI component is clearly identified in the discrepancy log. (b) Each MMI component as described in paragraph 2.10 (1) , or any MMI component installed and required to operate correctly to meet the current Statement of Qualification,

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-8 must be repaired or replaced within 30 calendar days, unless otherwise required or authorized by the MSP. (c) Notifying the MSP of any MMI that is not repaired within 30 days. (3) Pursuant to subsection 606.03 (4) of the CARs, no FSTD qualification certificate remains in force unless it maintains performance, and function in accordance with the applicable QPS, except in the cases set out in a Simulator Component Inoperative Guide (SCIG). (4) Each Air Operator Certificate holder, Private Operator Certificate holder, company organization or private citizen using the FSTD is responsible for developing a SCIG that reflects their operation and training program. Guidance for developing and using a SCIG is found at Attachment 2-1. The operator may decide that the use of a SCIG is not operationally beneficial due to the structure or complexity of their training program. In the case where a SCIG is not used, training restrictions associated with the sponsor’s current list of MMI components must be used as follows: (a) The instructor, or delegate of the Minister on-site is responsible for assessing the impact of the MMI components on the training session and notify the TPAA of any short term adjustments to the training program. (b) If the effect of the MMI component prevents reasonable adjustments to the approved training program or prevents the conduct of a pilot proficiency check, then the instructor, or delegate of the Minister will follow the procedures at section 2.9. Note: In the absence of a SCIG, inoperative or malfunctioning simulator system such as visual system, motion system, flight control system, or a system or component necessary for the safety of the FSTD occupants is inoperative or malfunctioning, refer to paragraph 2.9 (3) . The suitability of the device for continued training with the malfunction will be determined by the MSP in consultation with the TPAA and sponsor. 2.11 Loss or partial loss of qualification. (1) Qualification Removal: The MSP may remove some or all of an FSTD qualification including the withdrawal of approval for use of an FSTD; or deny an application for a qualification if: (a) The sponsor has provided an incorrect statement, upon which the Transport Canada NSEP relied or could have relied, made in support of an application for a qualification or a request for approval for use. (b) The sponsor has provided an incorrect entry, upon which the Transport Canada NSEP relied or could have relied, made in any logbook, record, or report that is kept, made, or used to show compliance with any requirement for an FSTD qualification or an approval for use. (c) A FFS at Level C or Level D does not have equipment and appliances installed and operating to the extent necessary for the issuance of a type-rating or the conduct of a Pilot Proficiency Check. (d) A Level A or Level B FFS does not have equipment and appliances installed and operating to the extent necessary to support the simulator portion of training, testing and/or checking required for issuance of a type-rating or to the conduct of a Pilot Proficiency Check. (e) The MSP has received notification from a Delegate of the Minister that action has been taken under section 2.9 to restrict the use of an FSTD due to a MMI component and the sponsor fails to correct the condition within 30 days.

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-9 (f) If a Delegate of the Minister, while conducting or monitoring training, informs the MSP that long term and/or multiple minor discrepancies on the FSTD are compromising the quality and effectiveness of the overall training. (2) Immediate Suspension. If the MSP determines that a circumstance exists which constitutes a threat to aviation safety, security, or the safe operation of the FSTD, the MSP will take the following immediate action: (a) Withdraw some or all of the FSTD’s qualifications to mitigate the threat, and make the withdrawal of qualification effective on the day the sponsor receives notice. (b) In the notice to the sponsor, the MSP articulates the reasons for its finding that immediate action is required to mitigate a threat to aviation safety, security, or the safe operation of the FSTD, which makes it impracticable or contrary to the public interest to stay the effectiveness of the finding. (3) Automatic Qualification Loss. An FSTD qualification is automatically lost when any of the following occurs: (a) The FSTD is not used to support a Transport Canada approved flight training program for the past 18 months. (b) The FSTD is not inspected in accordance with subsection 606.03 (5) of the CARs. (c) The FSTD is physically moved from one location and installed in a different location, regardless of distance. (d) The MQTG is missing or otherwise not available and a replacement is not made within 30 days. 2.12 Notification of qualification loss. (1) Except as provided in paragraph 2.11 (2) , when the MSP determines that the FSTD no longer meets qualification standards, the following procedure applies: (a) The MSP notifies the sponsor in writing that the FSTD no longer meets some or all of its qualification standards. (b) The MSP sets a reasonable period (but not less than 7 days) within which the sponsor may submit written information, views, and arguments on the FSTD qualification. (c) After considering all material presented, the MSP notifies the sponsor about the determination with regard to the qualification of the FSTD. (d) When the MSP notifies the sponsor that some or all of the FSTD is no longer qualified, the action described in the notification becomes effective not less than 30 days after the sponsor receives that notice unless — (i) The MSP finds under paragraph 2.11 (2) of this section that immediate action is required to mitigate a threat to aviation safety or security or the safe operation of the FSTD, or that makes it impracticable or contrary to the public interest to delay the effectiveness of the finding. In such a case, the withdrawal of qualification is effective on the day the sponsor receives notification; or (ii) The sponsor appeals to the Director of Standards for reconsideration of the MSP finding under paragraph 2.12 (2) of this section. (2) When a sponsor seeks reconsideration of a decision from the MSP concerning the FSTD qualification, the following procedure applies: (a) The sponsor must appeal for reconsideration of that decision within 30 days of the date that the sponsor receives a notice that some or all of the FSTD is no longer qualified.

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-10 (b) The sponsor must address its appeal to the Director of Standards, Transport Canada. (c) An appeal for reconsideration, if filed within the 30-day period, suspends the effectiveness of the determination by the MSP that the FSTD is no longer qualified unless the MSP has found, under paragraph 2.11 (2) that immediate action is required. 2.13 Qualification restoration procedures (1) FSTD qualification lost under this section may be restored when one of the following provisions are met: (a) The FSTD successfully passes an evaluation for initial qualification, where the MSP has determined that a full evaluation for initial qualification is necessary; or (b) The FSTD successfully passes an evaluation for those elements of an initial qualification evaluation, as determined to be necessary by the MSP; or (c) The MSP accepts a letter of compliance from the sponsor in lieu of an evaluation. Note: In making the determinations described in section 2.13, the MSP considers factors including the reason for the loss of qualification, any repairs or replacements that may have to have been completed, the number of recurrent evaluations missed, the number of sponsor-conducted quarterly inspections missed, and the care that had been taken of the device since the loss of qualification. (2) If an FSTD qualification certificate issued based on a previous standard automatically loses its qualification under section 2.11 the following applies: (a) Its qualification may be restored under paragraph 2.13 (1) using the qualification basis (in terms of objective tests and subjective tests) against which the FSTD was originally evaluated and qualified provided that the re-qualification is conducted in less than (2) years (b) FSTD not restored under paragraph 2.13 (1) for two (2) years or more, then the qualification basis (in terms of objective tests and subjective tests) for the re-qualification will be those standards in effect and current at the time of re-qualification application. 2.14 FSTD objective data requirements. (1) The validation data package, which consists of all objective data and other material or elements to support an initial evaluation and qualification of an FSTD, must be submitted in a form and manner acceptable to the MSP. (2) Evaluation of FSTD performance and handling qualities shall be based on a validation data package that includes aircraft manufacturer’s flight test data and all relevant data developed after the type certificate was issued (e.g., data developed in response to an airworthiness directive) if such data results from a change in performance, handling qualities, functions, or other characteristics of the aircraft that must be considered for flight crewmember training, checking and currency pursuant to CAR requirements. The following exceptions apply: (a) The validation data package may contain flight test data from a source in addition to or independent of the aircraft manufacturer’s data in support of an FSTD qualification, provided that this data is gathered and developed by that source in accordance with flight test methods, including a flight test plan, as described in the applicable QPS. (b) The validation data package may also contain predicted data, engineering simulation data, data from pilot owner or pilot operating manuals, or data from public domain sources, provided this data is acceptable to the MSP. If found acceptable the data may then be used in particular applications for FSTD qualification.

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-11 (c) Data requirements for non-type specific FTDs (Level 1, and 2) are addressed separately at Appendix E. (3) The MSP may require additional objective data, which may necessitate flight testing, if the validation data package does not support FSTD qualification requirements as described at paragraph 2.14 (2) and the applicable QPS appendix. (4) The sponsor must notify the MSP when they learn, or are advised that the aircraft manufacturer or data provider has additional, amended or revised data that may relate to FSTD performance or handling characteristics. 2.15 Interim qualification of FSTDs for new aircraft types or models (1) A sponsor may apply for and the MSP may issue an interim qualification level for an FSTD for a new type or model of aircraft, even though the aircraft manufacturer's aircraft data package is preliminary, if the sponsor provides the following in accordance with the application requirements at Chapter 3, Section 3.6: (a) The aircraft manufacturer's data, which consists of at least predicted data, validated by a limited set of flight test data; (b) The aircraft manufacturer's description of the prediction methodology used to develop the predicted data; and (c) The QTG test results. (2) An FSTD that has been issued interim qualification is deemed to have been issued initial qualification unless the MSP rescinds the qualification. The interim qualification terminates two years after it is issued, unless the MSP determines that specific conditions warrant otherwise. (3) Within twelve months of the release of the final aircraft data package by the aircraft manufacturer, but no later than two years after the issuance of the interim qualification status, the sponsor must apply for initial qualification in accordance with Chapter 3, Section 3.6 based on the final aircraft data package approved by the aircraft manufacturer, unless the MSP determines that specific conditions warrant otherwise. (4) An FSTD with interim qualification may be modified only in accordance with section 2.16 of this manual. 2.16 Modifications to FSTDs (1) Description of a modification . For the purposes of this manual, an FSTD is said to have been modified when: (a) Equipment or devices intended to simulate aircraft appliances are added to or removed from the FSTD, which change the MQTG or the Qualification Certificate issued by the Minister; or (b) Changes are made to either software or hardware that are intended to impact flight or ground dynamics; changes are made that impact performance or handling characteristics of the FSTD (including motion, visual, control loading, or sound systems for those FSTD levels requiring sound tests and measurements); or changes are made to the MQTG. Note: Routine software or hardware changes, or changes to the MQTG which do not affect required objective testing results or validation data approved during the initial evaluation of the FSTD are not considered modifications under this section. (2) FSTD Directive . An FSTD Directive may be issued if the Minister determines that an FSTD modification is necessary due to: (a) Safety of flight reasons;

Chapter 2 - Policies and procedures Page 2-12 (b) An amendments to Part VI or Part VII of the CARs that affects training; or (c) An airworthiness directive affecting the aircraft type, model or series number represented by the FSTD that affects training. (3) The sponsor of each affected FSTD must ensure that modifications are implemented according to the FSTD Directive regardless of the original qualification standards applicable to any specific FSTD. (4) Using the modified FSTD . The sponsor may not use, or allow the use of, or offer the use of, the FSTD with the proposed modification for pilot training or checking pursuant to CAR requirements until the approval process at Chapter 3, Section 3.4 of this manual is completed. 2.17 FSTD qualification based on a Bilateral Aviation Safety Agreement. (1) Bilateral agreements facilitate the reciprocal airworthiness certification of civil aeronautical products imported/exported between two signatory countries. A Bilateral Airworthiness Agreement (BAA) or Bilateral Aviation Safety Agreement (BASA) with Implementation Procedures for Airworthiness (IPA) provides for airworthiness technical cooperation between the Transport Canada and its counterpart national aviation authorities (NAA). Simulator Implementation Procedure (SIP) sets out the technical and procedural terms for mutual cooperation, technical assistance, and acceptance of for each other's systems and standards for flight simulator qualification evaluations. (2) The MSP may issue a Transport Canada FSTD certificate to an eligible sponsor based on the evaluation and qualification of a contracting State to the Convention on International Civil Aviation for an FSTD located in that contracting State provided that: (a) There is a BASA between Canada and the Contracting State that issued the original qualification; and (b) There is a Simulator Implementation Procedure (SIP) established under the BASA; and (c) The SIP contains any conditions and limitations on validation and issuance of such qualification by the TC.

Attachment 2-1 – Simulator Component inoperative Guide Page 2-13 Attachment 2-1 – Simulator Component Inoperative Guide Purpose (1) The Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs) state that each aircraft simulator in an approved training and checking program shall maintain the performance, functional and other characteristics required for approval. This means that each simulator must operate with all components operational at all times. If at any time its performance is degraded for any reason, the approval is void and any training or checking completed on the simulator while it is in this condition is invalid. (2) Some training and checking could be completed with certain components inoperative if relief were provided to the simulator approval requirements. While the aircraft Minimum Equipment List (MEL) is an important tool in training, especially in Line Oriented Flight Training (LOFT), it is not a practical relief vehicle. It relates directly to flight safety and airworthiness issues while the real issue is quality of training and not, strictly speaking, flight safety. Therefore, the MEL is not to be used to determine simulator training or checking status and another method of providing relief is required. Relief from the initial simulator approval requirements is permitted through the use of a Simulator Component Inoperative Guide (SCIG) or by following malfunctioning, or inoperative (MMI) procedures at Section 2.10 of Chapter 2. (3) Though the SCIG is concerned mainly with relief for full flight simulators, a SCIG can be prepared, approved and used with a training device. Typically a SCIG will focus on relief associated with simulator system malfunctions (i.e. visual, motion, controls, IOS etc.) however a SCIG may be drafted as comprehensively as the operator deems appropriate. MMI procedures at Section 2.10 of Chapter 2 provide a more flexible approach for air operators when dealing with systems of complex aircraft systems, or when using simulators from third party training providers. Application for Use of the SCIG (1) The individual operator (the Air Operator Certificate holder, company organization or private citizen using the simulator), is responsible for a SCIG that reflects their operation/training program. For example, one operator may train and check to Category II/III limits while another may train and check only to Category I limits; therefore, the second operator could use relief from Category II/III related to an inoperative component. It also may be possible to permit the use of FFS as a fixed based FTD if the visual or motion system is inoperative. (2) Once the operator has prepared a SCIG, using the example in this Attachment as a guide, it shall be submitted to the MSP for approval. The MSP will review it for compliance with this manual and forward it to the operational authority for approval. (3) When approval is obtained, the SCIG will become part of the operator’s training program. The SCIG must be readily available for review for each simulator training or checking session. Procedures for Using the SCIG (1) Any component or subpart of a simulator that is intentionally made inoperative for the purpose of training or checking by inserting a malfunction on the instructor's console is not considered inoperative for the purpose of the SCIG. (2) Each component that becomes inoperative shall be recorded in the maintenance log book for that simulator and its impact on the approved status of the device is to be determined using the SCIG if the FSTD is to continue training. Any system or subpart that is not listed in the guide shall be operational at all times when training for credits or checking is being conducted. All components and systems are required to operate for all checking, except as noted under "Remarks" in Table 2-1.

Attachment 2-1 – Simulator Component inoperative Guide Page 2-14 (3) Inoperative components will be documented and treated as an MMI and must be repaired within 30 days. (4) When a component becomes inoperative and the "Situation" column in Table 2-1 states "no training or checking", this means that the training credits and checking authorized for that phase of simulator are not allowed until the component is repaired. SCIG Description (1) An example SCIG is contained in Table 2-1. This is an example for an aeroplane simulator; however, the same format and related content can be used for rotorcraft simulators and FTDs. (2) Table 2-1 lists the major simulator components, the operational condition of the component, the phase of simulator the component applies to, the category the simulator is placed in because of the component's condition and prescribes the action that is required for training or checking, if authorized. (3) When a component becomes inoperative the simulator will be placed in one of the following categories: (a) no training or checking; (b) training under specific conditions; or (c) checking (4) An explanation of the column headings from Table 2-1 is as follows: (a) Component - a principal essential part such as the radios, performance instruments, engine instruments, system control panels, motion system, visual system or control loading that is computer operated, including the computer. (b) Situation - indicates which component or subpart has failed or deteriorated below initial qualification standards. (c) Level - refers to the approved level of the simulator only and indicates to which level of simulator the inoperative component applies. (d) Categories - are restrictions or authorizations placed on the simulator when a component becomes inoperative. Remarks: contains the conditions that must be met for training in specific conditions or when checking is authorized. (5) The following definitions are applicable to Table 2-1: (a) No Training or Checking - means that the training credits and checking that were authorized in that level of simulator are not allowed with the component inoperative. (b) Training in Specific Conditions - means some training is permitted if certain conditions are met as stated under the "Remarks" column in Table 2-1. (c) Checking - means any checking for a flight crew member licence, rating, type rating, LOFT, regency of experience, night take-off and landings and proficiency checks.
