Chapter 3 - Sponsor Administrative Procedures – Applications and Notifications Page 3-1 Chapter 3 Sponsor Administrative Procedures - Applications and Notifications 3.1 General (1) The sponsor will initiate applications by sending a “letter of intent” to the Manager, Simulator Program (MSP) or Regional Authority. A letter of intent is required for: (a) All Flight Simulation Training Device (FSTD) initial, upgrade, and foreign evaluations, (b) A change of FSTD sponsor, (c) FSTD relocation, and (d) Notifications of modifications that may require an update or special evaluation. (2) Prior to an evaluation scheduled in response to a letter of intent, the sponsor’s management representative must provide a signed “letter of compliance” to confirm they have verified that the FSTD is ready for an evaluation. The letters will be submitted as per the processes and requirements in this Chapter. (3) The subjective tests and objective tests that form the basis for a letter of compliance must be accomplished at the sponsor's training facility or other sponsor designated location where training will take place, except as provided for in the applicable QPS. (4) The pilot(s) contributing to a letter of compliance must: (a) Be designated by the sponsor; and (b) Be qualified in; (i) The aircraft or set of aircraft being simulated, or (ii) For aircraft not yet issued a type certificate, or aircraft not previously operated by the sponsor or not having previous Transport Canada-approved training programs conducted by the sponsor, an aircraft similar in size and configuration. (5) An FSTD sponsor or FSTD manufacturer may submit a request to the Minister for approval of a deviation from the QPS requirements as defined in this manual. (a) Requests for deviation must be submitted in a form and manner acceptable to the Minister and must provide an alternate means of compliance that meets or exceeds the testing requirements and tolerances as specified in the applicable QPS or will otherwise not adversely affect the fidelity and capability of the FSTDs evaluated and qualified under the deviation. (b) The Minister may consider deviation from the minimum requirements tables, the objective testing tables, the functions and subjective testing tables, and other supporting tables and requirements in the applicable QPS. (c) Deviations may be issued to an FSTD manufacturer for the initial qualification of multiple FSTDs, subject to terms and limitations as determined by Minister. Approved deviations will become a part of the permanent qualification basis of the individual FSTD and will be noted in the FSTD's Statement of Qualification. 3.2 Acceptance of Validation Data (1) Except in the case of interim qualifications, flight test data sources supplied by the aircraft manufacturer or validation data used on FSTD of the same aircraft type previously qualified by

Chapter 3 - Sponsor Administrative Procedures – Applications and Notifications Page 3-2 Transport Canada NSEP, FAA NSP or EASA will be reviewed and accepted as part of the initial qualification evaluation in accordance with the applicable QPS. (2) Independent data providers . The MSP must review and accept validation data packages generated from a source independent of aircraft manufacturer's data before it is used in support of an FSTD qualification. The review will verify that this data is gathered and developed by that source in accordance with flight test methods, including a flight test plan, as described in the applicable QPS. 3.3 Application for Initial or Upgrade Evaluations. (1) The sponsor seeking to qualify an FSTD must provide the MSP access to the FSTD for the length of time necessary for the NSEP to complete the required evaluation of the FSTD for initial qualification, which includes the conduct and evaluation of objective and subjective tests, including general FSTD requirements, as described in the applicable QPS, to determine that the FSTD meets the standards in that QPS. (2) Reinstating a Qualification . Sponsors requesting an initial evaluation to re-instate an FSTD qualification that was lost due to a voluntary suspension, relocation, or sponsor change will follow the application procedures for an initial evaluation in this section: (a) The MSP may decide to conduct a special evaluation in lieu of an initial evaluation if a reduced-scope evaluation is deemed sufficient to re-instate the qualification. The MSP will be determine the scope and focus of each special evaluation on a case-by-case basis. (b) If a qualification has been removed under paragraph 2.11 (1) or immediately suspended under paragraph 2.11 (2) , the MSP will follow the procedures at section 2.13 to restore the qualification. (3) Application process . The application process for an initial, upgrade, or interim qualification evaluation will be administered according to the following steps: (a) Letter of Intent . For each FSTD, the sponsor must submit a “letter of intent” requesting an initial qualification evaluation to the MSP through the appropriate regional or national office no later than 120 days prior to the evaluation date requested.) The letter will include A description of the FSTD; (i) The anticipated qualification level of the FSTD; (ii) The make, model, and series of aircraft simulated; and any other pertinent information. (iii) Request for approval to use an earlier standard as may be permitted in paragraph 2.5 (2) ; (iv) Any requests for deviations from the standard and/or alternate means of compliance to specific requirements set out in the applicable QPS; and (v) Any additional information that may affect the scope of the evaluation (i.e. FSTD relocation, sponsorship change, restoration after voluntary suspension etc.) Note: Requirements at sections 3.2 or 3.7 may be applicable if the sponsor intends to use validation data from sources independent of the aircraft manufacturer, or request an interim qualification for a new aircraft, to avoid any qualification delays, the sponsor should contact the MSP as early as possible to coordinate a review and acceptance of the validation data package. Note: For Non-Type Specific FTDs “letters of intent” refer to Chapter 6. (b) NSEP response . The MSP or delegated regional office will reply to the letter of intent within 15 business days with the following information;

Chapter 3 - Sponsor Administrative Procedures – Applications and Notifications Page 3-3 (i) Tentative dates for the initial evaluation; (ii) The date the sponsor must submit the QTG if applicable; (iii) A response to sponsor requests to; use an earlier standard, deviate from the applicable QPS, or use an alternate means of compliance; and (iv) An attached “qualification profile” form to be completed and returned to the MSP with or before the QTG submission. (v) Any special equipment and qualified personnel needed to accomplish or assist in the accomplishment of tests during initial qualification. (c) QTG Review. The Sponsor will submit the QTG (including validation data) in the form and manner described in the applicable QPS. The MSP will review the QTG and forward comments and questions resulting from the review to the Sponsor for their response. Depending on the results of the review, the MSP will confirm or postpone the evaluation date. The sponsor will provide a response to the QTG review comments no later than 5 working days before the evaluation date. (d) Letter of Compliance. The Sponsor will submit a “letter of compliance” signed by the management representative no later than 5 working days before the evaluation confirming that: (i) Qualified pilot(s), meeting the requirements of paragraph 3.1 (3) , after having flown all of the Operations Tasks listed in the applicable QPS appendix relevant to the qualification level of the FSTD, have determined that the performance and handling qualities of the FSTD represent those of the aircraft or set of aircraft within the normal operating envelope. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. The name of the pilot(s) making this determination must be identified on the letter of compliance. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. (ii) Qualified pilot(s), meeting the requirements of paragraph 3.1 (3) , or person(s) trained on simulator systems/sub-systems and trained on the operation of the simulated aircraft systems, after having exercised the operation of the FSTD and the pertinent functions available through the Instructor Operating Station(s) have determined that: FSTD systems and sub-systems (including the simulated aircraft systems) functionally represent those in the aircraft or set of aircraft; and the cockpit represents the configuration of the specific type or aircraft make, model, and series aircraft being simulated, as appropriate. The name of the person(s) making this determination must be available to the MSP upon request. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. (4) When the FSTD passes an evaluation for initial qualification, the MSP issues a Qualification Certificate that includes all of the following: (a) A Transport Canada Identification number (TCID); (b) Identification of the sponsor; (c) Identification of the make, model, and series of the aircraft or set of aircraft being simulated; (d) Identification of the configuration of the aircraft or set of aircraft being simulated (e.g., engine model or models, flight instruments, or navigation or other systems); (e) A statement that the FSTD is qualified as either a full flight simulator or a flight training device; (f) Identification of the qualification level of the FSTD;

Chapter 3 - Sponsor Administrative Procedures – Applications and Notifications Page 3-4 (g) A statement that (with the exception of the noted exclusions for which the FSTD has not been subjectively tested by the sponsor or the MSP and for which qualification is not sought) the qualification of the FSTD includes the tasks set out in the applicable QPS appendix relevant to the qualification level of the FSTD; and Note: Examples of the exclusions for which the FFS might not have been subjectively tested by the sponsor or the MSP and for which qualification might not be sought or granted include wind- shear training; circling approaches; upset training etc. (h) A statement referencing any deviations that have been granted and included in the permanent qualification basis of the FSTD. (5) After the NESP completes the evaluation for initial qualification, the sponsor must update the Qualification Test Guide (QTG), with the results of the Transport Canada-witnessed tests together with the results of all the objective tests described in the applicable QPS. (6) Upon issuance of the Qualification Certificate the updated QTG becomes the Master Qualification Test Guide (MQTG). The MQTG must be made available to the MSP upon request. 3.4 Notification of FSTD Modifications and updates. (1) The sponsor must notify the MSP in writing at least 21 days prior to making a modification to an FSTD described in paragraph 2.16 (1) of this manual. If the modification removes, increases, or changes the training qualifications identified on the Qualification Certificate, the sponsor must also notifying the TPAA of each Canadian air operator or private operator using the FSTD. (2) MQTG updates. The sponsor must update the MQTG with current objective test results and appropriate objective data each time an FSTD is modified and an objective test or other MQTG section is affected by the modification. If an FSTD Directive is the cause of this update, the direction to make the modification and the record of the modification completion must be filed in the MQTG. (3) Notification and approval process. The notification and approval process for an update or modification is as follows: (a) Letter of Intent . For each FSTD, the sponsor will submit a “letter of intent” to the MSP that: (i) Provides a description of the modification or update; (ii) Identifies any procedural, functional or physical change to the FSTD that may affect pilot training and checking; (iii) Identifies impact flight or ground dynamics; changes are made that impact performance or handling characteristics of the FSTD; (iv) Identifies any required changes to the MQTG; and (v) Provides a date when the modification or update would be available for evaluation. (b) NSEP response. The MSP or delegated regional office will reply to the letter of intent within 5 business days with the following; (i) Whether an update evaluation is required, (ii) Tentative date and scope of the update evaluation if required, (iii) Any special equipment and qualified personnel needed to accomplish or assist in the accomplishment of tests during the update evaluation, and (iv) Any additional requirements for approval if an update evaluation is deemed unnecessary.

Chapter 3 - Sponsor Administrative Procedures – Applications and Notifications Page 3-5 Note: Depending on the complexity and impact on training, the MSP may approve a modification based on a letter of compliance from the sponsor. (c) Letter of Compliance. The Sponsor will submit a “letter of compliance” signed by the management representative no later than 5 working days before a modification is implemented or evaluated confirming that: (i) Qualified pilot(s), meeting the requirements of paragraph 3.1 (3), after having flown the relevant Operations Tasks and determined that the modification or update represent those of the aircraft or set of aircraft within the normal operating envelope. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. The name of the pilot(s) making this determination must be identified on the letter of compliance. (ii) Qualified pilot(s), meeting the requirements of paragraph 3.1 (3) or person(s) trained on simulator systems/sub-systems and trained on the operation of the simulated aircraft systems, after having exercised the operation of the FSTD and the pertinent functions available through the Instructor Operating Station(s) have determined that: FSTD modification or update functionally represents those in the aircraft or set of aircraft; and all affected QTG tests are in tolerance. The name of the person(s) making this determination must be available to the MSP upon request. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. (d) Approval. The MSP will approve the use of a modification when: (i) The FSTD successfully passes a special evaluation according to the scope defined by the MSP in the response to the letter of intent; or (ii) The MSP has notified the sponsor that the letter of compliance has been accepted in lieu of an evaluation; and (iii) The Qualification Certificate has been appropriately amended. 3.5 Application for Foreign Evaluations (1) Unless otherwise deemed in the interest of the Minister, the MSP will only accept requests for foreign evaluations if the eligibility requirements at paragraph 2.6 (2) of this manual are satisfied. (2) Application process. The application process for a foreign initial evaluation is as follows: (a) Letter of Intent. Applicants requesting an initial qualification evaluation of an FSTD located outside of Canada must submit a “letter of intent” to the MSP and the applicant’s TPAA no later than 120 days prior to the evaluation date requested. The letter will include: (i) A description of the FSTD to include - manufacturer, current qualification level, the make / model and series of aircraft simulated; (ii) Information to justify the need for the FSTD in the applicant’s approved training program and the date the applicant wishes to begin training; (iii) the foreign sponsor’s name (FSTD operator), address, and contact information of the management representative; (iv) A copy of the National Authority’s latest qualification Certificate and evaluation report; (v) A statement that the applicant has read and understood the eligibility requirements at paragraph 2.6 (2) ; and (vi) Contact information for the applicant and their Transport Canada TPAA.

Chapter 3 - Sponsor Administrative Procedures – Applications and Notifications Page 3-6 (b) NSEP response. After reviewing the applicant’s request with their TPAA and the foreign sponsor, the MSP will reply to the letter of intent with the following; (i) Whether the request for a foreign evaluation is accepted; (ii) Tentative dates for the initial evaluation; (iii) The date the foreign sponsor must submit the QTG if applicable; (iv) Any qualified personnel and/or support from the applicant and sponsor needed to coordinate or complete the initial qualification. Note: The applicant is responsible for coordinating acceptable dates and FSTD slots (between 0800 and 1630 local time) with the FSTD sponsor and the NSEP. The dates of the evaluation are contingent upon the FSTD sponsor’s scheduling constraints and ability to support scope of evaluation required by the MSP. (c) Cost-recovery contract. Before the MSP commits any resources to the evaluation, the applicant must sign an agreement for recovering the incremental costs of providing services outside of Canada (form 26-0622 (0710-03), and provide a cost estimate to the applicant if requested. (d) Evaluation Plan. The MSP will inform foreign sponsor of the scope of the evaluation, and coordinate a test plan to verify QPS requirements. All correspondence with the sponsor will be copied to the applicant. (e) On-Site Evaluation. Upon successful completion of the evaluation, the MSP will issue the sponsor a qualification certificate and copy the applicant and their TPAA. Before leaving the facility, the evaluator will brief the sponsor on the administrative procedures and responsibilities to maintain the FSTD’s continuing qualification in accordance with this manual. (f) Recurrent evaluations. Before planning an evaluation for continuing qualification, the MSP will verify that the applicant has used the FSTD during the past 12 months and receive written confirmation from the applicant that they wish to continue the agreement for recovering the incremental costs of providing services outside of Canada. Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-4 4.4 Validation Test Tolerances - Non-Flight-Test Data (1) The objective-test tolerances listed in Appendix A2, Table A2A (aeroplanes) and Appendix B2, Table B2A (rotorcraft) provide a measureable means to compare and assess simulator performance against data acquired through actual flight-tests. Good engineering judgment should be applied to all tolerances in any test. A test fails when the results fall outside of the prescribed tolerance(s). (2) In some cases, engineering simulator data or other non-flight-test data sources may be considered if sound technical reasons or high costs prohibit the acquisition of flight-test data, or if alternative technical solutions are being proposed. If the use engineering data or non-flight-test data is allowed, then the data provider must supply a well-documented mathematical model and test procedure. (3) Engineering simulator data is deemed acceptable since the same simulation models used to generate the reference data are also used to test the FTSD. The expected test results from both devices should therefore be very similar. For this reason, the expected tolerance for FSTD objective tests validated using engineering data is reduced to 40% of those tolerances published in this manual for corresponding tests using flight-test data. However, there may be circumstances where the simulator models employed, or the manner in which they are integrated in the test loop, yield a higher fidelity than those supplied by the data provider. In these cases, it is possible that an error greater than 40% may be acceptable if the sponsor can provide adequate explanation. The MSP may accept that the results from the two sources exceed 40% tolerance band based on justification relating to: (a) Hardware (avionics units and flight controls); (b) Iteration rates; (c) Execution order; (d) Integration methods; (e) Processor architecture; (f) Digital drift, including: (g) Interpolation methods; (h) Data handling differences; or (i) Auto-test trim tolerances. 4.5 Validation Data Roadmap (1) A Validation Data Roadmap (VDR) is a document that contains guidance material from the data supplier recommending the best possible sources of data to be used as validation data in the QTG. The VDR should include rationale or explanation in test cases when; data or parameters are missing, engineering simulation data are to be used, flight test methods require

Additionally, the document should refer to other appropriate sources of validation data (e.g., sound and vibration data documents). (3) A sample Validation Data Roadmap (VDR) is shown in Attachment 4.1 to this Chapter. It depicts a generic roadmap matrix identifying sources of validation data for an abbreviated list of tests. A complete matrix should address all test conditions and provide actual data and data sources. 4.6 Acceptance Guidelines for Alternative Avionics (Flight-Related Computers and Controllers) (1) For a new aircraft type, the majority of flight validation data are collected on the first certified aircraft configuration with a “baseline” avionics ship-set. These data are then used to validate all flight simulators representing that aircraft type. Examples of such systems are; flight control computers, controllers for engines, autopilots, braking systems, nosewheel steering systems, and related avionics such as augmentation systems. (2) The MSP may require additional validation data for a FSTD with avionic hardware designs that differ from the baseline configuration, or if a software revision differs from a previously validated configuration. The QTG for a FSTD with additional or alternate avionics configurations should contain selected objective test cases and data to validate any significant performance differences attributed to the avionics configuration. (3) Approval Guidelines for Validating Alternate Avionics. The MSP will apply the following guidelines when qualifying FSTDs representing aircrafts with a revised avionics configuration, or more than one avionics configuration: (a) The baseline validation data should be based on flight test data, except where other data are specifically allowed (e.g., engineering flight simulator data). (b) The sponsor is responsible for determining and disclosing whether validation data used in the QTG is affected by an alternative avionics fit. (c) Validation data from the previously validated avionics configuration may be used provided that: (i) Avionics system or component changes do not affect QTG results. This includes updates to avionics systems that are tied to aircraft response but do not affect QTG results (e.g., the avionics change is a Built-In-Test-Equipment (BITE) update or a modification in a different flight phase). The QTG should include authoritative justification from the aircraft manufacturer or system supplier that this avionics change does not affect the test; or (ii) No new functionality is added and the impact of the avionics change on the aircraft response is demonstrated to be small based on acceptable and proven aeronautical principles. This should be supplemented with avionics-specific validation data from the aircraft manufacturer's engineering simulation, using the revised avionics configuration. The QTG should include an explanation of the change and its effect on the aircraft response. (4) Supplemental flight test data is required to validate the alternate avionics revision if: (a) An avionics change significantly affects some QTG results, or (b) New functionality is added to the avionics system. Note: Additional flight test validation data may not be needed if the avionics changes were certified without the need for testing with a comprehensive flight instrumentation package. The

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-6 aircraft manufacturer should coordinate flight simulator data requirements in advance with the MSP. (5) The Validation Road Map in the QTG should be amended to reflect the appropriate validation data source for each test. The roadmap should identify the revision state of the avionics systems that could affect specific test responses. 4.7 Control Dynamics (1) General. The characteristics of a flight control system have a major effect on an aircraft’s handling qualities. Pilot “feel” is a significant and important consideration when designing and accepting an aircraft flight control system or mechanism so that pilots will be comfortable and will consider the aircraft desirable to fly. In order for an FFS to be representative, it must “feel” like the aircraft being simulated. The fidelity requirements of an FFS control system is determined by recording and comparing the control feel dynamics of the FFS to actual aeroplane measurements taken in takeoff, cruise and landing configurations; or rotorcraft measurements in the hover and cruise configurations. (2) Recordings such as free response to an impulse or step function are classically used to estimate the dynamic properties of electromechanical systems. The ability to accurately estimate the dynamic properties depends how well the true inputs and responses are measured. Therefore, it is imperative that the best possible data be collected so that the FFS control loading system can be tuned to closely match to the aircraft system. The required dynamic control tests are described in Appendix A2, Table A2A (aeroplanes) and Appendix B2, Table B2A (rotorcraft). (3) For initial and upgrade evaluations, the QPS requires that control dynamics characteristics be measured and recorded directly from the flight controls. This procedure is usually accomplished by measuring the free response of the controls using a step or impulse input to excite the system. The procedure should be accomplished: (a) For aeroplanes - in the takeoff, cruise and landing flight conditions and configurations (Handling Qualities - Appendix A2, Table A2A), or (b) For rotorcraft - in the hover and cruise flight conditions and configurations for rotorcraft (Handling Qualities - Appendix B2, Table B2A). (4) For aircraft with irreversible control systems, measurements may be obtained on the ground if proper pitot-static inputs are provided to represent airspeeds typical of those encountered in flight. Likewise, it may be shown that for some aeroplanes or rotorcraft, different flight configurations have like effect on control measurements. Thus, one may suffice for another. If either or both considerations apply, engineering validation or aircraft manufacturer rationale should be submitted as justification for ground tests or for eliminating a particular configuration required in the QPS. For FFSs requiring static and dynamic tests at the controls, special test fixtures will not be required during initial and upgrade evaluations if the QTG shows both test fixture results and the results of an alternate approach (e.g., computer plots that were produced concurrently and show satisfactory agreement). Repeat of the alternate method during the initial evaluation satisfies this test requirement. (5) Control Dynamics Evaluations. The dynamic properties of control systems are often stated in terms of frequency, damping, and a number of other classical measurements. In order to establish a consistent means of validating test results for FFS control loading, criteria are needed that will clearly define the measurement interpretation and the applied tolerances. Criteria are needed for underdamped, critically damped and overdamped systems. In the case of an underdamped system with very light damping, the system may be quantified in terms of frequency and damping. In critically damped or overdamped systems, the frequency and damping are not readily measured from a response time history. Therefore, the following suggested measurements may be used:

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-7 (a) For Levels C and D simulators. Tests to verify that control feel dynamics represent the aircraft should show that the dynamic damping cycles (free response of the controls) match those of the aircraft within specified tolerances. The MSP recognizes that several different testing methods may be used to verify the control feel dynamic response. The MSP will consider the merits of testing methods based on reliability and consistency. One acceptable method of evaluating the response and the tolerance to be applied is described below for the underdamped and critically damped cases. A sponsor using this method to comply with the QPS requirements should perform the tests as follows: (i) Underdamped Response. Two measurements are required for the period, the time to first zero crossing (in case a rate limit is present) and the subsequent frequency of oscillation. It is necessary to measure cycles on an individual basis in case there are non-uniform periods in the response. Each period will be independently compared to the respective period of the aircraft control system and, consequently, will enjoy the full tolerance specified for that period. The damping tolerance will be applied to overshoots on an individual basis. Care should be taken when applying the tolerance to small overshoots since the significance of such overshoots becomes questionable. Only those overshoots larger than 5 percent of the total initial displacement should be considered significant. The residual band, labeled T(Ad) on Figure I is ±5 percent of the initial displacement amplitude Ad from the steady state value of the oscillation. Only oscillations outside the residual band are considered significant. When comparing FFS data to aircraft data, the process should begin by overlaying or aligning the FFS and aircraft steady state values and then comparing amplitudes of oscillation peaks, the time of the first zero crossing, and individual periods of oscillation. The FFS should show the same number of significant overshoots to within one when compared against the aircraft data. The procedure for evaluating the response is illustrated in Figure II. (ii) Critically damped and Overdamped Response. Due to the nature of critically damped and overdamped responses (no overshoots), the time to reach 90 percent of the steady state (neutral point) value should be the same as the aircraft within ±10 percent. The simulator response must be critically damped also. Figure II illustrates the procedure. (iii) Special considerations. Control systems that exhibit characteristics other than classical overdamped or underdamped responses should meet specified tolerances. In addition, special consideration should be given to ensure that significant trends are maintained.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-10 (3) Alternate Method for Control Dynamics Evaluation of Flight Controls with Atypical Response. Dynamic responses exhibiting atypical behaviour, as frequently seen on reversible controls, may be evaluated using an alternate reference line better suited for such cases. This alternate line is based on the dynamic response itself and attempts to better approximate the true rest position of the control throughout the step response. (4) A flight control dynamic response is considered atypical when it does not exhibit classic second order system behaviour. For underdamped systems, the key features of such a behaviour are: a constant period, decaying overshoots (an overshoot is always smaller than the previous one) and a fixed steady state position. Overdamped systems show a control position that will demonstrate a smooth exponential decay from its initial displacement towards a fixed steady state position. (5) The following is a full discussion on how to compute the alternate reference line. Figure III shows the final result and how to apply the tolerances using the new reference. (a) Background. When evaluating a flight control dynamic response, the periods, amplitudes and residual band are defined with respect to a reference line, which is the steady state value of the control. This selection is made since it is assumed that the steady state value is representative of the control’s rest position throughout the test. For standard irreversible control systems this is very often a valid assumption. However, in the case of reversible control systems for example, aerodynamic forces on the control surfaces influence the instantaneous rest position of the control. During the dynamic test, the control’s rest position will vary in response to the variance of the flight conditions. In such a case, the instantaneous rest position and steady state value at the end of the test are not equivalent. When the tolerances are applied to the entire dynamic response based on the steady state value, they may become incorrect and lead to problems evaluating the cases. (b) Alternate Reference Line. In such cases, an alternate reference line may be used, which attempts to better approximate the true rest position of the control throughout a step response. The alternate reference line is obtained as follows: (i) On the control position curve, identify median points, defined as points on the control position curve located equidistantly between two consecutive peaks, measured vertically (see Figure 4-3). The last median point is the first point where the dynamic portion of the response has ended rather than the mid-point between the last peak and the end of the dynamic portion. (ii) Join the median points to produce the “line of medians.” Then, identify reference points, defined as the intersection of a vertical line passing through a position peak and the line of medians (see Figure 4-4). (iii) The first reference point is the last control position before the start of the excitation. When this part of the data is not available, project the first available reference point horizontally to time zero. The last reference point is simply the last median point. (iv) Link all the reference points to obtain the alternate reference line (see Figure 4- 4), and append the final non-dynamic portion to it Note: The rest position is defined as the position where the aeroplane control or rotorcraft blade would eventually settle if no pilot force were applied to it (left free). This position may or may not be affected by the aerodynamic conditions, the aircraft configuration and the accelerations it is subjected to. It will depend on the type of flight control system in the aircraft. Typically, reversible control systems will be affected while irreversible systems will not. The instantaneous rest position is defined as the theoretical rest position at a particular point in time and at the same conditions of that moment.

The parameters chosen for FFS validation should indicate these changes. (a) A dedicated test should be provided that will validate the aerodynamic ground effect characteristics. (b) The organization performing the flight tests may select appropriate test methods and procedures to validate ground effect. However, the flight tests should be performed with enough duration near the ground to sufficiently validate the ground-effect model. Note: Ground Effect requirements are not applicable to Level A simulators since landing credits may not be included in Level A simulator training. (2) The MSP will consider the merits of testing methods based on reliability and consistency. Acceptable methods of validating ground effect are described below. If other methods are proposed, rationale should be provided to conclude that the tests performed validate the ground- effect model. A sponsor using the methods described below to comply with the QPS requirements should perform the tests as follows: (a) Level fly-bys. The level fly-bys should be conducted at a minimum of three altitudes within the ground effect, including one at no more than 10% of the wingspan above the ground, one each at approximately 30% and 50% of the wingspan where height refers to main gear tire above the ground. In addition, one level-flight trim condition should be conducted out of ground effect (e.g., at 150% of wingspan). The shallow approach landing should be performed at a glide slope of approximately one degree with negligible pilot activity until flare. (3) The lateral-directional characteristics are also altered by ground effect. For example, because of changes in lift, roll damping is affected. The change in roll damping will affect other dynamic modes usually evaluated for FFS validation. In fact, Dutch roll dynamics, spiral stability, and roll- rate for a given lateral control input are altered by ground effect. Steady heading sideslips will also be affected. These effects should be accounted for in the FFS modeling. Several tests such as crosswind landing, one engine inoperative landing, and engine failure on take-off serve to validate lateral-directional ground effect since portions of these tests are accomplished as the aircraft is descending through heights above the runway at which ground effect is an important factor. 4.9 Motion Systems (1) General. Pilots use continuous information signals to regulate the state of the aircraft. In addition to the instruments and outside-world visual information, a FFS must also provide pilots whole- body motion feedback to provide essential vestibular that allow the pilot to quickly and accurately react to aircraft dynamic changes, particularly in the presence of external disturbances. (2) The motion system should meet basic objective performance criteria, and should be subjectively tuned at the pilot's seat position to represent the linear and angular accelerations of the aircraft during a prescribed minimum set of maneuvers and conditions. The response of the motion cueing system should also be repeatable. (3) The Motion System tests in Section 3 of Appendix A2 Table A2A (aeroplanes), and Appendix B2, Table B2A (rotorcraft) are intended to qualify the FFS motion cueing system from a mechanical performance standpoint. Additionally, the list of motion effects provides a representative sample of dynamic conditions that should be present in the flight simulator. An additional list of representative, training-critical maneuvers, selected from Section 1 (Performance tests), and Section 2 (Handling Qualities tests), in Table A2A (aeroplanes) and Table B2A (rotorcraft), that should be recorded during initial qualification (but without tolerance) to indicate the flight simulator motion cueing performance signature have been identified (reference Section 3.e). These tests are intended to help improve the overall standard of FFS motion cueing. (4) Motion System Checks. The intent of test 3a, Frequency Response, and test 3b, Turn-Around Check, as described in the Table of Objective Tests, are to demonstrate the performance of the motion system hardware, and to check the integrity of the motion set-up with regard to calibration and wear. These tests are independent of the motion cueing software and should be considered robotic tests. (5) Motion System Repeatability. The intent of this test is to ensure that the motion system software and motion system hardware have not degraded or changed over time. This diagnostic test should be completed during continuing qualification checks in lieu of the robotic tests. This will allow an improved ability to determine changes in the software or determine degradation in the hardware. The following information delineates the methodology that should be used for this test. (a) Input: The inputs should be such that rotational accelerations, rotational rates, and linear accelerations are inserted before the transfer from aircraft center of gravity to pilot reference point with a minimum amplitude of 5 deg/sec/sec, 10 deg/sec and 0.3 g, respectively, to provide adequate analysis of the output. (b) Recommended output: (i) Actual platform linear accelerations; the output will comprise accelerations due to both the linear and rotational motion acceleration; (ii) Motion actuators position.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-14 (iii) Motion Cueing Performance Signature. (6) Background. The intent of this test is to provide quantitative time history records of motion system response to a selected set of automated QTG maneuvers during initial qualification. It is not intended to be a comparison of the motion platform accelerations against the flight test recorded accelerations (i.e., not to be compared against aircraft cueing). If there is a modification to the initially qualified motion software or motion hardware, (e.g., motion washout filter, simulator payload change greater than 10%) then a new baseline may need to be established. (7) Test Selection. The “conditions” in Section 3.e. Appendix A2, Table A2A (aeroplanes) and Appendix B2, Table B2A (rotorcraft) are intended to identify those maneuvers where motion cueing is the most discernible. These are general tests applicable to all types of aircraft and should be completed for motion cueing performance signature at any time acceptable to the MSP prior to or during the initial qualification evaluation, and the results included in the MQTG. (8) Priority. Motion system should be designed with the intent of placing greater importance on those maneuvers that directly influence pilot perception and control of the aircraft motions. For the maneuvers identified in Section 3.e. Appendix A2, Table A2A (aeroplanes) and Appendix B2, Table B2A (rotorcraft), the flight simulator motion cueing system should have a high tilt co- ordination gain, high rotational gain, and high correlation with respect to the aircraft simulation model. (9) Data Recording. The minimum list of parameters provided should allow for the determination of the flight simulator's motion cueing performance signature for the initial qualification evaluation. The following parameters are recommended as being acceptable to perform such a function: (a) Flight model acceleration and rotational rate commands at the pilot reference point; (b) Motion actuators position; (c) Actual platform position; (d) Actual platform acceleration at pilot reference point. (10) Motion Vibrations. (a) Presentation of results. The characteristic motion vibrations may be used to verify that the flight simulator can reproduce the frequency content of the aircraft when flown in specific conditions. The test results should be presented as a Power Spectral Density (PSD) plot with frequencies on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis. The aircraft data and flight simulator data should be presented in the same format with the same scaling. The algorithms used for generating the flight simulator data should be the same as those used for the aircraft data. If they are not the same then the algorithms used for the flight simulator data should be proven to be sufficiently comparable. As a minimum, the results along the dominant axes should be presented and a rationale for not presenting the other axes should be provided. (b) Interpretation of results. The overall trend of the PSD plot should be considered while focusing on the dominant frequencies. Less emphasis should be placed on the differences at the high frequency and low amplitude portions of the PSD plot. During the analysis, certain structural components of the flight simulator have resonant frequencies that are filtered and may not appear in the PSD plot. If filtering is required, the notch filter bandwidth should be limited to 1 Hz to ensure that the buffet feel is not adversely affected. In addition, a rationale should be provided to explain that the characteristic motion vibration is not being adversely affected by the filtering. The amplitude should match aircraft data as described below. However, if the PSD plot was altered for subjective reasons, a rationale should be provided to justify the change. If the plot is on a logarithmic scale, it may be difficult to interpret the amplitude of the buffet in terms of acceleration. For example, a 1 × 10−3 g -rms2/Hz would describe a heavy buffet and may be seen in the deep stall regime. Alternatively, a 1 × 10−6 g -r ms2/Hz buffet is almost not perceivable; but may represent a flap buffet at low speed. The previous two examples

On a PSD plot this represents three decades (one decade is a change in order of magnitude of 10; and two decades is a change in order of magnitude of 100). Note: In the example, “g-rms2 is the mathematical expression for “g's root mean squared. Initial (and Upgrade) Qualification Requirements. 4.10 Sound System (1) General. The total sound environment in the aircraft is very complex, and changes with atmospheric conditions, aircraft configuration, airspeed, altitude, and power settings. Flight deck sounds are an important component of the flight deck operational environment and provide valuable information to the flight crew. These aural cues can either assist the crew (as an indication of an abnormal situation), or hinder the crew (as a distraction or nuisance). For effective training, the flight simulator should provide flight deck sounds that are perceptible to the pilot during normal and abnormal operations, and that are comparable to those of the aircraft. The flight simulator operator should carefully evaluate background noises in the location where the device will be installed. To demonstrate compliance with the sound requirements, the objective or validation tests in the applicable QPS were selected to provide a representative sample of normal static conditions typically experienced by a pilot. (2) Alternate propulsion . For FFS with multiple propulsion configurations, any condition listed in Table A2A (aeroplane) or B2A (rotorcraft) should be presented for evaluation as part of the QTG if identified by the aircraft manufacturer or other data supplier as significantly different due to a change in propulsion system (engine or propeller). (3) Data and Data Collection System. (a) Information provided to the flight simulator manufacturer should comply be presented in the format suggested by the “International Air Transport Association (IATA) Flight Simulator Design and Performance Data Requirements,” as amended. This information should contain calibration and frequency response data. (b) The system used to perform the tests listed in Table A2A (aeroplane) or B2A (rotorcraft) should comply with the following standards: (i) The specifications for octave, half octave, and third octave band filter sets may be found in American National Standards Institute (ANSI) S1.11-1986. (ii) Measurement microphones should be type WS2 or better, as described in International Electro-technical Commission (IEC) 1094-4-1995. (iii) Headsets. If headsets are used during normal operation of the aircraft they should also be used during the flight simulator evaluation. (iv) Playback equipment. Playback equipment and recordings of the QTG conditions should be provided during initial evaluations. (v) Background noise: (c) Background noise is the noise in the flight simulator that is not associated with the aircraft, but is caused by the flight simulator's cooling and hydraulic systems and extraneous noise from other locations in the building. Background noise can seriously impact the correct simulation of aircraft sounds, and should be kept below the aircraft sounds. In some cases, the sound level of the simulation can be increased to compensate for the background noise. However, this approach is limited by the specified tolerances and by the subjective acceptability of the sound environment to the evaluation pilot.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-16 (i) The acceptability of the background noise levels is dependent upon the normal sound levels in the aircraft being represented. Background noise levels that fall below the lines defined by the following points, may be acceptable: (A) 70 dB @ 50 Hz; (B) 55 dB @ 1000 Hz; (C) 30 dB @ 16 kHz. Note: These limits are for un- weighted 1⁄3 octave band sound levels. Meeting these limits for background noise does not ensure an acceptable flight simulator. Aircraft sounds that fall below this limit require careful review and may require lower limits on background noise. (d) Validation testing. Deficiencies in aircraft recordings should be considered when applying the specified tolerances to ensure that the simulation is representative of the aircraft. Examples of typical deficiencies are: (i) Variation of data between tail numbers. (ii) Frequency response of microphones. (iii) Repeatability of the measurements.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-18 4.11 Transport Delay Testing (1) The following explains how to measure the “total transport delay” and “introduced-transport delay” (induced by the flight simulator systems) to determine whether overall system time response time does not exceed QPS tolerance requirements. The transport delay should be measured from control inputs through the interface, through each of the host computer modules and back through the interface to motion, flight instrument, and visual systems. (2) Measurement of transport delay and application of QPS tolerances will depend on the FSTD system architecture, which can be categorized as follows: (a) Simulation of classic non-computer controlled aircraft. Figure 4-6 illustrates the total transport delay for a non-computer-controlled aircraft or the classic transport delay test. (i) Introduced transport delay is measured from the flight deck control input to the reaction of the instruments and motion and visual systems. (ii) Since there are no aircraft-induced delays for this case, the total transport delay is equivalent to the introduced delay. (3) Simulation of computer controlled aircraft using real aircraft controller black boxes . Figure 4-7 illustrates the transport delay testing method using the real aircraft controller system. (a) The control input may also be introduced after the aircraft controller system and the introduced transport delay measured directly from the flight control interface input to the reaction of the instruments, and simulator motion and visual systems. (b) To obtain the introduced transport delay for the motion, instrument and visual signal, the delay induced by the aircraft controller should be subtracted from the total transport delay. (c) This difference represents the introduced delay and should not exceed the standards prescribed in Appendix A1, Table A1A (aeroplanes) or Appendix B1, Table B1A (rotorcraft). (4) Simulation of computer controlled aircraft using software emulation of aircraft boxes. Figure 4-8 illustrates the transport delay testing method used on a flight simulator that uses a software emulated aircraft controller system. (a) It is not possible to measure the introduced transport delay using the simulated aircraft controller system architecture for the pitch, roll and yaw axes. Therefore, the signal should be measured directly from the pilot controller. (b) The flight simulator manufacturer should measure the total transport delay and subtract the inherent delay of the actual aircraft components because the real aircraft controller system has an inherent delay provided by the aircraft manufacturer. (c) The flight simulator manufacturer should ensure that the introduced delay does not exceed the standards prescribed in Appendix A1, Table A1A (aeroplanes) or Appendix B1, Table B1A (rotorcraft). (5) Simulation using software avionics or re-hosted instruments . Special measurements for instrument signals are required for flight simulators using a real aircraft instrument system or simulated or re-hosted instruments. Figures 4-9a and 4-9b illustrate the transport delay testing method for each case. (a) Figure 4-9a illustrates the transport delay measurement for a real aircraft instrument display system (without aircraft display simulation). The introduced transport delay is the delay between the control movement and the instrument change on the data bus and is obtained by subtracting the inherent delay of the actual aircraft components from the total transport delay. The inherent delay of the aircraft between the data bus and the displays is indicated in figure 4-9. The display manufacturer should provide this delay time.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-19 (b) Figure 4-9b illustrates the modified testing method required to measure introduced transport delay due to software avionics or re-hosted instruments. The total simulated instrument transport delay is measured and the aircraft hardware delay is subtracted from this total. This difference represents the introduced transport delay. (c) The introduced delay should not exceed the tolerances in Table A1A (aeroplanes) or B1A (rotorcraft). (6) Recorded signals. The signals recorded to conduct the transport delay calculations should be explained on a schematic block diagram. The flight simulator manufacturer should also provide an explanation of why each signal was selected and how they relate to the above descriptions. (7) Interpretation of results. Flight simulator results vary over time from test to test due to “sampling uncertainty.” All flight simulators run at a specific rate where all modules are executed sequentially in the host computer. The flight controls input can occur at any time in the iteration, but these data will not be processed before the start of the new iteration. For example, a flight simulator running at 60 Hz may have a difference of as much as 16.67 msec. between test results. This does not mean that the test has failed. Instead, the difference is attributed to variations in input processing. In some conditions, the host simulator and the visual system do not run at the same iteration rate, so the output of the host computer to the visual system will not always be synchronized. (8) The transport delay test should account for both daylight and night modes of operation of the visual system. In both cases, the tolerances prescribed in Table A1A must be met and the motion response should occur before the end of the first video scan containing new information.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-21 4.12 Visual Display Systems (1) This section applies to all FSTDs with a cross-cockpit display installation, meaning a display that can be viewed as a continuous image from any location in the cockpit. For the purpose of this section: (a) “Collimated display” will be used as a generic term for a display system that provides an image apparently located at a distance substantially further away from the pilot than the physical dimensions of the display system, and (b) “Direct projected display” refers to a display system with an image actually located on a screen in front of the pilot. (2) Collimated display: This is a display system that projects its image on a screen via a large concave mirror. The position and curvature of the mirror places an image on the screen that appears at a distance greater than 10 m (33 ft) from the observer. This is the maximum distance that human eyes can effectively judge distance using binocular cues (stereopsis), beyond which all rays from the object are perceived as being effectively parallel. The collimated display causes the viewer's eyes to focus at infinity creating an illusion that objects are located at a distance (see Figure 4-10). As a result, regardless of the viewing angle or eye point position, objects projected at a significant distance from the viewer will behave geometrically in the same way as they would in the real world. Typically, a collimated display provides an image located not closer than about 20-33 ft (6-10 m) from the viewer, with the distance varying over the field-of-view. (a) Collimated displays are well suited to many simulation applications where the area of interest is located relatively distant from the observer and the viewing angles to objects are effectively independent of the cockpit eye point position. Consider the view of the runway seen by the flight crew lined up on an approach. In the real world, the runway is distant and the light rays from the runway to the eyes are parallel (see Figure 4-10). The runway appears to be straight ahead from both flight crew positions. Note that the distance to the runway has been shortened for clarity. If drawn to scale, the runway would be farther away and the rays from the two seats would be closer to being parallel. (b) While the horizontal field-of-view of a collimated display can be extended to approximately 210°-220°, the vertical field-of-view has been limited to about 40°-45°. These limitations result from tradeoffs in optical quality and interference between the display components and flight deck structures, but were sufficient to meet FFS regulatory approval for rotorcraft FFSs. However, recent designs have been introduced with vertical fields of view of up to 60° for rotorcraft applications. (3) Direct projected display: This is a non-collimated (or dome) display system that projects the image directly onto a screen approximately 3m from the observer. The screen may be cylindrical or spherical in shape, depending on the field of view required. From the observer’s perspective, the image will appear and behave as if all the objects in the scene are located on the screen surface. When compared to a collimated display, the orientation of the image presented by a direct projected display will change with the pilot’s viewing angles; however it will produce a more representative image at near-field viewing. (a) The effect of viewing angle in a direct projected display is shown in Figure 4-11. The image orientation can be aligned for only one eye point at a time. The visual system in the Figure 4-11 has been aligned for the right seat eye point position and the runway appears to be straight ahead of the aircraft for this viewer. For the left seat viewer, however, the runway appears to be somewhat to the right of the aircraft. When the aircraft moves towards the runway, the velocity vector will be directed towards the runway and the left-seat pilot will be perceive a yaw offset. (b) In the case of near field objects, a collimated display will cause the pilot to misinterpret objects that are close to the aircraft as being at a distance. This perception error can be

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-22 significantly reduced in a direct projected display, making the visual simulation close to the ground, typically encountered in rotorcraft operational training, more representative. (c) The field-of-view possible with a direct projected display can be larger than that of a collimated display. Depending on the configuration, a field-of-view of 240° by 90° is possible and can be exceeded. Note: The minimum radius of the screen and the position of the cockpit relative to the screen may be determined from the allowed angular errors for the pilot(s). In the example illustrated by Figure 4-12, if the criterion is to have no more than 10° offset for both pilots simultaneously, then for an eye point at the centre of a spherical screen, where the pilots’ eye spacing is a typical 1.168 m (46 in.), the screen radius must be at least 1.168/(2*Tan10°) = 3.312 m (10.9 ft). (4) Additional display considerations (a) While the situations described above are for discrete viewing positions, the same arguments can be extended to moving eye points produced by the viewer's head movement. In the real world, the parallax effects resulting from head movement provide distance cues. The effect is particularly strong for relative movement of flight deck structure in the near field and modeled objects in the distance. Collimated displays will provide accurate parallax cues for distant objects, but increasingly inaccurate cues for near field objects. The situation is reversed for dome displays. (b) Stereopsis cues resulting from the different images presented to each eye for objects relatively close to the viewer also provide depth cues. Again, the collimated and dome displays provide more or less accurate cues depending on the modeled distance of the objects being viewed. (5) Training implications (a) In view of the basic principles described above, it is clear that neither display approach provides a completely accurate image for all possible object distances. The sponsor should consider the training role of the FFS when configuring the display system to make the optimum choice. Factors that should be considered include relative importance of training tasks at low altitudes, the role of the two crew members in the flying tasks, and the field-of-view required for specific training tasks. (b) Both display types have their strengths, and any choice will be a “trade-off” to gain the best fit to the training requirement. The topics can be summarized as: (c) The image distance issues do not represent the only factor to be considered. Neither display type is ideal for rotorcraft simulation. The availability of peripheral cues and the level of details in the scene are also very important. Rich scene information is now available from high quality image generators and this capability is likely to improve. (d) When an operation is required with a crew of two pilots, collimated displays may be the preferred choice unless a large vertical field of view is essential. (e) For single pilot operation, direct projection is likely to be the optimum solution. (f) If a direct projected system is used for a multi-pilot operation then one pilot would be designated as “pilot flying” and the other as “pilot not flying”. The image generator could then be set up to ensure that only the pilot flying has the correct view (bearing in mind that the maximum offset allowed for the pilot not flying is 20°). Should it be required to switch the “pilot flying” function to the other pilot, the image could be re-aligned to give the correct view to the new “pilot flying” eye point. A two-pilot training operation using a direct projection system may be best served without offsetting the eye point, i.e. with both pilots having up to 10° offset. (g) The TPAA’s decision on when to permit a centrally aligned display for pilot training and checking will depend upon:

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-23 (i) The criticality of the specific training or checking maneuver; (ii) The need for the handling pilot to use linear visual features; and (iii) The need to reinforce an effective skill transfer for maneuvers that can only be trained or checked in the FSTD.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-24 4.13 Visual Scene Requirements. (1) When the simulator is being used by an instructor or evaluator for purposes of training, checking, or testing under this chapter, only airport models classified as Class I, Class II, or Class III may be used by the instructor or evaluator. These classification of airport models are defined as follows: (a) Class I. Whether modeling real world or fictional airports (or landing areas for helicopters), these airport models (or landing areas for helicopters) are those that meet the requirements of Table A3B of Appendix A3 for aeroplanes and Table B3B of Appendix B3 for rotorcraft, as appropriate, and are evaluated by the National Simulator Evaluation Program (NSEP), and are listed on the FSTD Qualification Certificate. (b) Class II . Whether modeling real world or fictional airports (or landing areas for helicopters), these airport models (or landing areas for helicopters) are those models that are in excess of those used for simulator qualification at a specified level. The FSTD sponsor is responsible for determining that these models meet the requirements set out in Table A3C of Appendix A3 for aeroplanes and Table B3C of Appendix B3 for rotorcraft, as appropriate. (c) Class III . This is a special class of airport model (or landing area for helicopters), used for specific purposes, and includes models that may be incomplete or inaccurate when viewed without restriction, but when appropriate limits are applied (e.g., ‘‘valid for use only in visibility conditions less than 1⁄2 statue mile or RVR2400 feet,’’ ‘‘valid for use only for approaches to Runway 22L and 22R’’), those features that may be incomplete or inaccurate may not be able to be recognized as such by the crewmember being trained, tested, or checked. Class III airport models used for training, testing, or checking activities under this Chapter requires the certificate holder to submit to the TPAA an appropriate analysis of the skills, knowledge, and abilities necessary for competent performance of the task(s) in which this particular model is to be used, and requires TPAA acceptance of each Class III model. (2) Except for special use airport models, described as Class III, all airport models required by this chapter must be representations of real-world, operational airports or representations of fictional airports and must meet the requirements set out in Tables A3B or A3C of Appendix A3 for aeroplanes and Tables B3B or B3C of Appendix B3 for rotorcraft, as appropriate. (3) If fictional airports are used, the sponsor must ensure that navigational aids and all appropriate maps, charts, and other navigational reference material for the fictional airports (and surrounding areas as necessary) are compatible, complete, and accurate with respect to the visual presentation of the airport model of this fictional airport. An SOC must be submitted that addresses navigation aid installation and performance and other criteria (including obstruction clearance protection) for all instrument approaches to the fictional airports that are available in the simulator. The FSTD Qualification Certificate must reference and account for information in the terminal instrument procedures manual and the construction and availability of the required maps, charts, and other navigational material. This material must be clearly marked “for training purposes only.” (4) Neither Class II nor Class III airport visual models are required to appear on the FSTD Qualification Certificate. The sponsor is responsible for keeping instructors and evaluators apprised of the airport models that meet Class II or Class III requirements on any given simulator. The method or process used by the sponsor to achieve this must be available for review by the TPAA and NSEP. Class II models may be subject to review during recurrent evaluations. (5) When an airport model represents a real world airport and a permanent change is made to that real world airport (e.g., a new runway, an extended taxiway, a new lighting system, a runway closure) without a written extension grant from the MSP (described in paragraph 4.13.6 of this section), an update to that airport model must be made in accordance with the following time limits:

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-29 flight time experience in that aircraft) and knowledgeable about the operation of the aircraft and the operation of the FFS. 4.15 Alternative Data Sources, Procedures, and Instrumentation: Level A and Level B Simulators Only (1) Sponsors are not required to use the alternative data sources, procedures, and instrumentation; however, a sponsor may choose to use one or more of the alternative sources, procedures, and instrumentation described in Table A2B for Aeroplanes or Table B2B for Rotorcraft. Note: There is no Level-A qualification level published in this manual for a Rotorcraft FFS. (2) It has become standard practice for experienced simulator manufacturers to use modeling techniques to establish data bases for new simulator configurations while awaiting the availability of actual flight test data. The data generated from the aerodynamic modeling techniques is then compared to the flight test data when it becomes available. The results of such comparisons have become increasingly consistent, indicating that these techniques, applied with the appropriate experience, are dependable and accurate for the development of aerodynamic models for use in Level A and Level B simulators. Based on this history of successful comparisons, the MSP has concluded that those who are experienced in the development of aerodynamic models may use modeling techniques as an alternative method for acquiring flight test data for Level A or Level B simulators. (3) The information in Tables A2B (Aeroplanes) and B2B (Rotorcraft) (Alternative Data Sources, Procedures, and Instrumentation) is presented to describe an acceptable alternative to data sources for simulator modeling and validation and an acceptable alternative to the procedures and instrumentation traditionally used to gather such modeling and validation data. (a) Alternative data sources that may be used for part or all of a data requirement are the Aircraft Maintenance Manual, the Airplane Flight Manual (AFM), Rotorcraft Flight manual (RFM), Aircraft Design Data, the Type Inspection Report (TIR), Certification Data or acceptable supplemental flight test data. (b) The sponsor should coordinate with the MSP prior to using alternative data sources in a flight test or data gathering effort. (c) The use of these alternative data sources, procedures, and instrumentation is based on the following presumptions: (i) For Aeroplanes FFS only: Data gathered through the alternative means does not require angle of attack (AOA) measurements or control surface position measurements for any flight test. However, AOA can be sufficiently derived if the flight test program ensures the collection of acceptable level, un-accelerated, trimmed flight data. All of the simulator time history tests that begin in level, un- accelerated, and trimmed flight, including the three basic trim tests and “fly-by” trims, can be a successful validation of angle of attack by comparison with flight test pitch angle. (Note: Due to the criticality of angle of attack in the development of the ground effects model, particularly critical for normal landings and landings involving cross-control input applicable to Level B simulators, stable “fly-by” trim data will be the acceptable norm for normal and cross-control input landing objective data for these applications.) (ii) The use of a rigorously defined and fully mature simulation controls system model that includes accurate gearing and cable stretch characteristics (where applicable), determined from actual aircraft measurements. Such a model does not require control surface position measurements in the flight test objective data in these limited applications.
