The sponsor may disregard those tests where stated flight or operating conditions do not apply to the simulated aircraft or qualification level (e.g., an engine out missed approach for a single-engine aircraft, or a hover test for a Level B rotorcraft simulator). Although use of a driver program designed to automatically accomplish the tests is encouraged for all simulators and required for Level C and Level D simulators, each test must be able to be accomplished manually while recording all appropriate parameters. (a) Computer-generated simulator test results are required for each test except where an alternative test is specifically authorized by the MSP. The results of each test must be: (b) presented to allow a clear comparison against the validation data described in Chapter 2, Section 2.14 of this manual; (c) produced on an appropriate recording device acceptable to the MSP and must include simulator number, date, time, conditions, tolerances, and appropriate dependent variables portrayed in comparison to the validation data; (d) presented as time histories unless otherwise indicated in Table A2A or Table B2A as applicable; and (e) labeled using the tolerances and units given. (2) Table A2A, Table B2A set out the test results required, including the parameters, tolerances, and flight conditions for simulator validation. Tolerances are provided for the listed tests because mathematical modeling and acquisition/development of reference data are often inexact. All tolerances listed in the following tables are applied to simulator performance. When two tolerance values are given for a parameter, the less restrictive value may be used unless otherwise indicated. In those cases where a tolerance is expressed only as a percentage, the tolerance percentage applies to the maximum value of that parameter within its normal operating range as measured from the neutral or zero position unless otherwise indicated. (3) Certain tests included in Appendix A2 (aeroplanes) and Appendix B2 (rotorcraft) must be supported with a Statement of Compliance (SOC). Requirements for SOCs are indicated in Table A1A or Table B1A as applicable.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-31 (4) When operational or engineering judgment is used to assess test results against flight test validation data, such judgment must not be limited to a single parameter. When it is difficult or impossible to match simulator to aircraft data throughout a time history, differences must be justified using valid comparisons of other related parameters for the condition being assessed. For example, data that exhibit rapid variations of a specific measured parameter may require interpolations or a “best fit” data selection. To accept the “best fit” and support an overall interpretation of the test, all relevant parameters related to the maneuver or flight condition must be provided. (5) The FFS may not be programmed so that the mathematical modeling is correct only at the validation test points. Unless noted otherwise, simulator tests must represent aircraft performance and handling qualities at operating weights and centers of gravity (CG) typical of normal operation. If a test is supported by aircraft data at one extreme weight or CG, another test supported by aircraft data at mid-conditions or as close as possible to the other extreme must be included; however, if it can be shown that a test is relevant only at one extreme CG or weight condition, then it need not be repeated at the other extreme. (6) When comparing the parameters listed to those of the aircraft, sufficient data must also be provided to verify the correct flight condition and aircraft configuration changes. For example, to show that control force is within ±0.5 pound (0.22 daN) in a static stability test, data to show the correct airspeed, power, thrust or torque, aircraft configuration, altitude, and other appropriate datum identification parameters that make affect the tolerance parameter must also be given. If comparing short period dynamics, normal acceleration may be used to establish a match to the aircraft, but airspeed, altitude, control input, aircraft configuration, and other appropriate data must also be given. All airspeed values must be properly annotated (e.g., indicated versus calibrated). In addition, the same variables must be used for comparison (e.g., compare inches to inches rather than inches to centimeters). (7) The QTG provided by the sponsor must clearly describe how the simulator will be set up and operated for each test. Each simulator subsystem may be tested independently; however, to assure that the total simulator system meets the prescribed standards, overall integrated testing of the system must also be accomplished. A manual test procedure with explicit and detailed steps for completing each test must also be provided. (8) The sponsor may request approval to use applicable tests and tolerances from this manual for a previously qualified simulator. The request must be made by submitting a proposed MQTG revision for MSP approval. Once approved, the revised tests may be used in subsequent continuing qualification evaluations. (9) Motion system tests will adhere to the following: (a) The minimum excursions, accelerations, and velocities for pitch, roll, and yaw must be measurable about a single, common reference point and must be achieved by driving one degree of freedom at a time. (b) The minimum excursions, accelerations, and velocities for heave, sway, and surge may be measured about different, identifiable reference points and must be achieved by driving one degree of freedom at a time. (10) Aeroplane FFS Only – Objective tests for Computer Controlled Aircraft (CCA) simulators, or other highly augmented aeroplane simulators, will require flight test data for the Normal (N) and/or Non- normal (NN) control states, as indicated in Appendix A2. Where test results are independent of control state, Normal or Non-normal control data may be used. All tests in Table A2A require test results in the Normal control state unless specifically noted otherwise in the Test Details section following the CCA designation. The MSP will determine what tests are appropriate for aeroplane simulation data. When making this determination, the MSP may require other levels of control state degradation for specific aeroplane tests. Where Non-normal control states are required, test data must be provided for one or more Non-normal control states, and must include the least

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-32 augmented state. Where applicable, flight test data must record Normal and Non-normal states for: (a) Pilot controller deflections or electronically generated inputs, including location of input; and (b) Flight control surface positions unless test results are not affected by, or are independent of, surface positions. (11) Tests of handling qualities must include validation of augmentation devices. FFSs for highly augmented aircraft will be validated both in the augmented configuration and the unaugmented configuration (or failure state with the maximum permitted degradation in handling qualities). The following guidelines apply: (a) Where various levels of handling qualities result from failure states, validation of the effect of the failure is necessary. (b) Unaugmented data are not required for those performance and static handling qualities tests if the design of the system precludes any effect on control position, and the control position is of primary concern in the test. (c) In those instances where the unaugmented aircraft response is divergent and non- repeatable, it may not be feasible to meet the specified tolerances. (d) Alternative requirements for testing will be mutually agreed upon by the sponsor and the MSP on a case-by-case basis. (12) Some tests will not be required for simulators using aircraft hardware in the simulator flight deck (e.g., “rotorcraft modular controller” or “aeroplane side stick controller”). These exceptions are noted in Appendix A2, Table A2A for aeroplanes and Appendix B2, Table B2A for rotorcraft. However, in these cases, the sponsor must provide a statement that the aircraft hardware meets the appropriate manufacturer's specifications and the sponsor must have supporting information to that fact available for MSP review. (13) The terms “light”, “medium”, and “near maximum” gross weight are defined in Chapter 1 of this manual. These definitions may not be appropriate for the simulation of light-class rotorcrafts. In cases where light-class rotorcrafts are being simulated, prior coordination with the MSP on acceptable weight ranges is required. (14) In those cases where the QPS permits a “snapshot” or a “series of snapshot” tests results in lieu of a time-history, the sponsor or other data provider must ensure that a steady state condition exists from interval of 4 seconds before to 1 second after the time the “snapshot” was captured. (15) If relevant winds are present in the objective data, the wind vector should be clearly noted as part of the data presentation, expressed in conventional terminology, and related to the runway being used for tests near the ground. (16) The numbering system used for objective test results in the QTG should closely follow the numbering system set out in Appendix A2, Table A2A (aeroplanes) or Appendix B2, Table B2A (rotorcraft) as applicable. 4.17 Subjective Testing Discussion (1) The subjective tests provide a means evaluate the simulator’s stability and performance over a typical training session. The tests are based on performing specific tasks to verify the correct operation of simulator controls, instruments, and systems and to determine whether the device accurately simulates required maneuvers, procedures, or tasks. These tasks are listed in the following Tables are intended for simulator evaluation purposes only. They may not be used to limit or exceed the authorizations for use of a given level of simulator, as described on the SOQ, or as approved by the TPAA:

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-33 (a) Tables A3A (Aeroplanes) and B3A (Rotorcraft) - Operations Tasks are used to organize and test the pilot’s functional interaction with the simulator. These tasks are divided into phases of flight and include maneuvers and procedures called flight tasks. While performing these tasks, the evaluator will also examine the sensory cueing from the motion system, visual system, and special effects in an operational context. There are flight tasks included to address some features of advanced technology aircrafts and innovative training programs. For example, “high angle-of-attack maneuvering” is included to provide a required alternative to “approach to stalls” for aircrafts employing flight envelope protection functions. (b) Tables A3G and B3G, Instructor Operating Station are tests that address the overall function and control of the simulator including the various simulated environmental conditions; simulated aircraft system operations (normal, abnormal, and emergency); visual system displays; and special effects necessary to meet flight crew training, evaluation, or flight experience requirements. (2) All simulated aircraft-system functions will be assessed for normal and, where appropriate, alternate operations. Normal, abnormal, and emergency operations associated with a flight phase will be assessed during the evaluation of flight tasks or events within that flight phase. Simulated aircraft systems are listed separately under “Any Flight Phase” to ensure appropriate attention to systems checks. Operational navigation systems (including inertial navigation systems, global positioning systems, or other long-range systems) and their associated electronic display systems will be evaluated if installed. The NSEP evaluation report will identify any operational discrepancies or system limitations observed during the evaluation. (3) Simulators demonstrating a satisfactory circling approach during the initial will be qualified for the circling approach maneuvers. The Sponsor must present a Class I or II scene with a circling approach to support the evaluation. To be considered satisfactory, the circling approach will be flown at maximum gross weight for landing, with minimum visibility for the aircraft approach category, and must allow proper alignment with a landing runway at least 90° different from the instrument approach course while allowing the pilot to keep an identifiable portion of the airport in sight throughout the maneuver. Once FSTD is qualified, the TPAA may approve the use of this approach in the sponsor's Transport Canada-approved flight training program. Additional circling approaches may be approved by a type-qualified Transport Canada Civil Aviation Inspector or Approved Check Pilot (ACP) by following the procedures and guidance found in Chapter 7, Section 7.8 of this manual. (4) At the request of the TPAA, the MSP may assess a device to determine if it is capable of simulating certain training tasks in a sponsor's training program that are not included in appendices A3 or B3. Unless directly related to a requirement for the qualification level, the results of such an evaluation would not affect the qualification level of the simulator. However, if the MSP determines that the simulator does not accurately simulate that training activity, the simulator would not be approved for that training activity. (5) The TPAA may allow the use of Class III airport models if the sponsor provides an appropriate analysis of the skills, knowledge, and proficiency necessary for competent performance of the tasks in which this particular model is used. The analysis should identify the specific airport model and describe the ability of the FFS/visual media to support the skill, knowledge and proficiency objectives of the particular training tasks in which it is used. The analysis should also specify the training conditions and script scenarios for training and checking and identify any limitations that may affect the training. 4.18 Conduct of Initial and Upgrade Evaluations (1) The MSP may only accept initial evaluation requests from eligible sponsors as defined in Chapter 2, Section 2.6 of this manual. However, other FFS evaluations may be conducted on a case-by- case as the Minister deems appropriate in accordance with pre-arranged conditions and agreements.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-34 (2) The MSP will conduct an evaluation as completely as possible for each FFS configuration. Each initial or upgrade evaluation will be based on assessing compliance to the general simulator requirements in Appendix A1 or B1, the objective tests listed in Appendix A2 (aeroplanes) or B2 (rotorcraft), and the subjective tests listed in Appendix A2 (aeroplanes) or B2 (rotorcraft), as applicable. The evaluations described herein will include, but not necessarily be limited to the following: (a) Aircraft responses, including longitudinal and lateral-directional control responses (see Appendix A2 (aeroplanes) or B2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (b) Performance in authorized portions of the simulated aircraft's operating envelope, to include tasks evaluated by the MSP in the areas of surface operations, takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, approach, and landing as well as abnormal and emergency operations (see Appendix A2 (aeroplanes) or B2 (rotorcraft)); (c) Control checks (see Appendix A1 and A2 (aeroplanes) or Appendix B1 and B2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (d) Flight deck configuration (see Appendix A1 (aeroplanes) or B1 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (e) Pilot, flight engineer, and instructor station functions checks (see Appendix A1 and A3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix B1 and B3 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (f) Aircraft systems and sub-systems (as appropriate) as compared to the aircraft simulated (see Appendix A1 and A3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix B1 and B3 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (g) FFS systems and sub-systems, including force cueing (motion), visual, and aural (sound) systems, as appropriate (see Appendix A1 and A2 (aeroplanes) or Appendix B1 and B2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); and (h) Certain additional requirements, depending upon the qualification level sought, including equipment or circumstances that may become hazardous to the occupants. The sponsor may be subject to Occupational Safety and Health Administration requirements. (3) The MSP administers the objective and subjective tests, which will includes an examination of system functions. The tests will include a qualitative assessment by a Transport Canada pilot. The NSEP evaluation team leader may assign other qualified personnel to assist in accomplishing the functions examination and/or the objective and subjective tests performed during an evaluation when required. (a) Objective tests provide a basis for measuring and evaluating FFS performance and determining compliance with the requirements of this part. (b) Subjective tests provide a basis for: (i) Evaluating the capability of the FFS to perform over a typical utilization period; (ii) Determining that the FFS satisfactorily simulates each required task; (iii) Verifying correct operation of the FFS controls, instruments, and systems; and (iv) Demonstrating compliance with the requirements of this manual. Note: Guidance for planning a functions and subjective test can be found at Attachment 4.2 of this chapter. (c) The tolerances for the test parameters listed in Appendix A2 (aeroplanes) and B2 (rotorcraft) reflect the range of tolerances acceptable to the MSP for FFS validation and are not to be confused with design tolerances specified for FFS manufacture. In making decisions regarding tests and test results, the MSP relies on the use of operational and engineering judgment in the application of data (including consideration of the way in which the flight test was flown and the way the data was gathered and applied), data presentations, and the applicable tolerances for each test.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-35 (d) Problems with objective test results are handled as follows: (i) If the NSEP evaluation team detects a problem with an objective test procedure, content or presentation during an evaluation, the test may be repeated or the discrepancy may be resolved by amending the QTG. (ii) If it is determined that the results of an objective test do not support the level requested but do support a lower level, the MSP may qualify the FFS at that lower level. For example, if a Level D evaluation is requested and the FFS fails to meet sound test tolerances, it could be qualified at Level C. (4) After an FFS is successfully evaluated, the MSP will issues a FSTD Qualification Certificate to the sponsor. The certificate will include a “qualification profile” that identifies the FFS software and appliances evaluated, and any additional tasks or deviations from the referenced tasks lists described in Appendix A1, Table A1B (aeroplanes) or Appendix B1, Table B1B (rotorcraft) as applicable. Once qualified, the FFS is eligible for use in a Transport Canada approved flight training program. The TPAA is the responsible authority that approves the use of an FSTD in a flight training program. It remains the sponsor’s responsibility to ensure TPAA approval for each air operator or private operator using the FFS in a Transport Canada approved training program. (5) Under normal circumstances, the MSP will tentatively schedule a date for the initial or upgrade evaluation within fifteen (15) working days after receiving the sponsor’s request (letter of intent) and confirm the evaluation date when the complete QTG is acceptable. Sponsor application procedures for initial evaluations are found in Section 3.3 of the manual. 4.19 Continuing Qualification Evaluations and Requirements (1) The MSP will conduct continuing qualification evaluations in accordance with the requirements of section 606.03 of the CARs unless the MSP becomes aware of discrepancies or performance problems with the device that warrants more frequent evaluations. (2) To support continuing qualification, the sponsor is responsible for: (a) conducting a minimum of four evenly spaced inspections throughout the year. The objective test sequence and content of each inspection must be developed by the sponsor and must be acceptable to the MSP. (b) maintaining a description of the functional pre-flight check in their maintenance procedures’ (c) recording all “functional pre-flights” in the FFS discrepancy log book or other acceptable location, and (d) maintaining a current record of any item found to be missing, malfunctioning, or inoperative. (3) The sponsor's test sequence and the content of each quarterly inspection required in chapter 2, paragraph 2.8.1 a) of this manual should include a balance and a mix from the objective test requirement areas listed as follows: (a) Performance. (b) Handling qualities. (c) Motion system (where appropriate). (d) Visual system (where appropriate). (e) Sound system (where appropriate). (f) Other FFS systems. (4) The sponsor must provide a person knowledgeable about the operation of the aircraft and the operation of the FFS to support a continuing qualification evaluation conducted by the MSP.

Chapter 4 – Full Flight Simulator – Qualification Performance Standards Page 4-36 (5) If the NSEP evaluator plans to accomplish specific tests during a normal continuing qualification evaluation that requires the use of special equipment or technicians, the sponsor will be notified as far in advance of the evaluation as practical; but not less than 72 hours. Examples of such tests include latencies, control dynamics, sounds and vibrations, motion, and/or some visual system tests. (6) The continuing qualification evaluations, described in Chapter 3, paragraph 3.8.3 of this manual will normally require 6 hours of FFS time. However, flexibility is necessary to address abnormal situations or situations involving aircraft with additional levels of complexity (e.g., computer controlled aircraft). The sponsor should anticipate that some tests may require additional time. The continuing qualification evaluations will consist of the following: (a) Review of the results of the quarterly inspections conducted by the sponsor since the last scheduled continuing qualification evaluation. (b) Review MQTG document control and relevant discrepancy history. (c) A selection of approximately 8 to 15 objective tests from the MQTG that provide an adequate opportunity to evaluate the performance of the FFS. The tests chosen will be performed either automatically or manually and should be able to be conducted within approximately one-third of the allotted FFS time. (d) A subjective evaluation of the FFS to perform a representative sampling of the tasks set out in Appendix A3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix B3 (rotorcraft) as applicable. This portion of the evaluation should take approximately two-thirds of the allotted FFS time. (e) An examination of the functions of the FFS may include the motion system, visual system, sound system, instructor operating station, and the normal functions and simulated malfunctions of the aeroplane systems. This examination is normally accomplished simultaneously with the subjective evaluation requirements. Note: Guidance for planning a functions and subjective test can be found at Attachment 4.2 of this chapter. (7) In addition to the scheduled continuing qualification evaluation, each FFS is subject to evaluations conducted by the MSP at any time without prior notification to the sponsor. Such evaluations would be accomplished in a normal manner (i.e., requiring exclusive use of the FFS for the conduct of objective and subjective tests and an examination of functions) if the FFS is not being used for pilot training and checking. However, if the FFS were being used, the evaluation would be conducted in a non-exclusive manner. This non-exclusive evaluation will be conducted by the FFS evaluator accompanying the ACP, instructor, or Transport Canada inspector aboard the FFS along with the student(s) and observing the operation of the FFS during the training, testing, or checking activities.

The sponsor should also consult the objective tests in Appendix A2 and functions and subjective tests listed in Appendix A3 of this to determine the complete requirements for an aeroplane specific level simulator. High Angle of Attack Modeling Aerodynamic stall modeling that includes degradation in static/dynamic lateral-directional stability, degradation in control response (pitch, roll, and yaw), uncommanded roll response or roll-off requiring significant control deflection to counter, apparent randomness or non-repeatability, changes in pitch stability, Mach effects, and stall buffet, as appropriate to the aircraft type. The aerodynamic model must incorporate an angle of attack and sideslip range to support the training tasks. At a minimum, the model must support an angle of attack range to ten degrees beyond the stall identification angle of attack. The stall identification angle of attack is defined as the point where the behavior of the aeroplane gives the pilot a clear and distinctive indication through the inherent flight characteristics or the characteristics resulting from the operation of a stall identification device (e.g., a stick pusher) that the aeroplane has stalled. The model must be capable of capturing the variations seen in the stall characteristics of the aeroplane (e.g., the presence or absence of a pitch break, deterrent buffet, or other indications of a stall where present on the aircraft). The aerodynamic modeling must support stall training maneuvers in the following flight conditions: (1) Stall entry at wings level (1g); (2) Stall entry in turning flight of at least 25° bank angle (accelerated stall); (3) Stall entry in a power-on condition (required only for propeller driven aircraft); and (4) Aircraft configurations of second segment climb, high altitude cruise (near performance limited condition), and approach or landing. A Statement of Compliance (SOC) is required which describes the aerodynamic modeling methods, validation, and checkout of the stall characteristics of the FSTD. The SOC must also include verification that the FSTD has been evaluated by a subject matter expert pilot acceptable to the FAA. See Chapter 6, Appendix E for detailed requirements. X X The requirements in this section only apply to those FSTDs that are qualified for full stall training tasks. Sponsors may elect to not qualify an FSTD for full stall training tasks; however, the FSTD’s qualification will be restricted to approach to stall training tasks that terminate at the activation of the stall warning system. Specific guidance should be available to the instructor which clearly communicates the flight configurations and stall maneuvers that have been evaluated in the FSTD for use in training. See Chapter 6, Appendix E for additional guidance material.

Appendix A1 – Aeroplane FFS – General Simulator Requirements Page 4-45 2.n. Upset Prevention and Recovery Training (UPRT). Aerodynamics Evaluation: The simulator must be evaluated for specific upset recovery maneuvers for the purpose of determining that the combination of angle of attack and sideslip does not exceed the range of flight test validated data or wind tunnel/analytical data while performing the recovery maneuver. The following minimum set of required upset recovery maneuvers must be evaluated in this manner and made available to the instructor/evaluator. Other upset recovery scenarios as developed by the FSTD sponsor must be evaluated in the same manner: (1) A nose-high, wings level aircraft upset; (2) A nose-low aircraft upset; and (3) A high bank angle aircraft upset. Upset Scenarios: IOS selectable dynamic aeroplane upsets must provide guidance to the instructor concerning the method used to drive the FSTD into an upset condition including any malfunction or degradation in the FSTD’s functionality required to initiate the upset. The unrealistic degradation of simulator functionality (such as degrading flight control effectiveness) to drive an aeroplane upset is not acceptable unless used purely as a tool for repositioning the FSTD with the pilot out of the loop. Instructor Operating System (IOS): The simulator must have a feedback mechanism in place to notify the instructor/evaluator when the simulator’s validated aerodynamic envelope and aircraft operating limits have been exceeded during an upset recovery training task. This feedback mechanism must include: (1) FSTD validation envelope. This must be in the form of an alpha/beta envelope (or equivalent method) depicting the “confidence level” of the aerodynamic model depending on the degree of flight validation or source of predictive methods The envelopes must provide the instructor real-time feedback on the simulation during a maneuver. There must be a minimum of a flaps up and flaps down envelope available; (2) Flight control inputs. This must enable the instructor to assess the pilot’s flight control displacements and forces (including fly-by-wire as appropriate); and (3) Aeroplane operational limits. This must display the aircraft operating limits during the maneuver as applicable for the configuration of the aeroplane. Statement of Compliance (SOC): An SOC is required that defines the source data used to construct the FSTD validation envelope. The SOC must also verify that each upset prevention and recovery feature programmed at the instructor station and the associated training maneuver has been evaluated by a suitably qualified pilot using methods described in this section. The statement must confirm that the recovery maneuver can be performed such that the FSTD does not exceed the FSTD validation envelope, or when exceeded, that it is within the realm of confidence in the simulation accuracy. FSTDs used to conduct upset recovery maneuvers at angles of attack above the stall warning system activation must meet the requirements for high angle of attack modeling as described in section 2.m. Special consideration should be given to the motion system response during upset prevention and recovery maneuvers. Notwithstanding the limitations of simulator motion, specific emphasis should be placed on tuning out objectionable motion system responses. Consideration should be taken with flight envelope protected aeroplanes as artificially positioning the aeroplane to a specified attitude may incorrectly initialize flight control laws. Appendix A2 – Aeroplane FFS – Objective Tests Page 4-58 Appendix A2 - Aeroplane FFS – Objective Tests I ntroduction (1) For the purposes of this appendix, the flight conditions specified in the Flight Conditions Column of Table A2A are defined as follows: (a) Ground—on ground, independent of aeroplane configuration; (b) Take-off—gear down with flaps/slats in any certified takeoff position; (c) First segment climb—gear down with flaps/slats in any certified takeoff position (normally not above 50 ft. AGL); (d) Second segment climb—gear up with flaps/slats in any certified takeoff position (normally between 50 ft. and 400 ft. AGL); (e) Clean—flaps/slats retracted and gear up; (f) Cruise—clean configuration at cruise altitude and airspeed; (g) Approach—gear up or down with flaps/slats at any normal approach position as recommended by the aeroplane manufacturer; and (h) Landing—gear down with flaps/slats in any certified landing position. (2) The format for numbering the objective tests must match those in Table A2A. When a test number (or series of numbers) is not required, the term “Reserved” is used in the table at that location. (3) If relevant winds are present in the objective data, the wind vector should be clearly noted as part of the data presentation, expressed in conventional terminology, and related to the runway being used for the test.

Appendix A2 – Aeroplane FFS – Objective Tests Page 4-142 Acceptance Guidelines for Alternative Engines Data (1) Background (a) For a new aeroplane type, the majority of flight validation data are collected on the first aeroplane configuration with a “baseline” engine type. These data are then used to validate all flight simulators representing that aeroplane type. (b) Implementing an engine-type from a different manufacturer or a design change that differs from the baseline engine into an FSTD may significantly affect some QTG test results. Additional flight test validation data may be needed for flight simulators representing an aeroplane with engines of a different type than the baseline, or for engines with thrust rating that is different from previously validated configurations. (c) To qualify a flight simulator with alternate engines, the QTG should contain tests validated against flight test data for selected cases where engine differences are expected to be significant. (2) Approval Guidelines for Validating Alternate Engine Applications . The following guidelines apply to flight simulators representing aeroplanes with alternate engine applications or with more than one engine type or thrust rating: (a) Validation tests can be segmented into two groups, those that are dependent on engine type or thrust rating and those that are not. (i) Tests that are independent of engine type or thrust rating can be based on validation data from any engine application. Tests in this category should be designated as independent of engine type or thrust rating. (ii) Tests that are affected by engine type. Test affected by engine type or thrust rating should be validated against engine-specific flight test data for each particular aeroplane-engine configuration. See Table A2C, Alternate Engine Validation Flight Tests in this section for a list of acceptable tests. (b) Alternate engine validation data should be based on flight test data, except if conditions at paragraphs 3a and 3b are not exceeded, or where other data are specifically allowed (e.g., engineering simulator/simulation data). (i) If certification of the flight characteristics of the aeroplane with a new thrust rating (regardless of percentage change) requires certification flight testing with a comprehensive stability and control flight instrumentation package, then the conditions described in Table A2C in this section should be obtained from flight testing and presented in the QTG. (ii) If the new thrust rating is certified on the aeroplane without need for a comprehensive stability and control flight instrumentation package, then flight test data, other than throttle calibration data, are not required (c) As a supplement to the engine-specific flight tests listed in Table A2C and baseline engine- independent tests, additional engine-specific engineering validation data should be provided in the QTG, as appropriate, to facilitate running the entire QTG with the alternate engine configuration. The sponsor and the MSP should agree in advance on the specific validation tests to be supported by engineering simulation data. (i) The QTG should include a supplementary Validation Road Map or matrix indicating the validation data source for each test using the alternate engine or thrust rating... (ii) The flight test conditions in Table A2C are appropriate and should be sufficient to validate implementation of alternate engines in a flight simulator.

Appendix A2 – Aeroplane FFS – Objective Tests Page 4-143 3) Test Requirements. The QTG must contain selected engine-specific flight test data sufficient to validate the alternative thrust level when: (a) The engine type is the same, but the thrust rating exceeds that of a previously flight-test validated configuration by five percent (5%) or more; or (b) The engine type is the same, but the thrust rating is less than the lowest previously flight- test validated rating by fifteen percent (15%) or more. See Table A2C for a list of acceptable tests. (c) Flight test data is not required if the thrust increase is greater than 5%, but flight tests have confirmed that the thrust increase does not change the aeroplane's flight characteristics. (d) Throttle calibration data (i.e., commanded power setting parameter versus throttle position) must be provided to validate all alternate engine types and engine thrust ratings that are higher or lower than a previously validated engine. Data from a test aeroplane or engineering test bench with the correct engine controller (both hardware and software) are required.

Nosewheel scuffing: Procedure: Taxi at various ground speeds and manipulate the nosewheel steering to cause yaw rates to develop that cause the nosewheel to vibrate against the ground (“scuffing”). Thrust effect with brakes set: Procedure: Set the brakes on at the take-off point and increase the engine power until buffet is experienced. Evaluate its characteristics. Mach and maneuver buffet: Procedure: With the simulated airplane trimmed in 1 g flight while at high altitude, increase the engine power so that the Mach number exceeds the documented value at which Mach buffet is experienced. Appendix B1 – Rotorcraft – Tasks vs Simulator Level – Subjective Requirements Page 4-178 Appendix B1 – Rotorcraft FFS – General Simulator Requirements. (1) This Appendix describes the general simulator requirements for qualifying a rotorcraft FFS. The sponsor should also consult the objective tests in Appendix B2 and functions and subjective tests listed in Appendix B3 of this to determine the complete requirements for an aeroplane specific level simulator. (2) The material contained in this Appendix is divided into the following categories: (a) General flight deck configuration. (b) Simulator programming. (c) Equipment operation. (d) Equipment and facilities for instructor/evaluator functions. (e) Motion system. (f) Visual system. (g) Sound system. (3) Table B1A provides the standards for the General Simulator Requirements. (4) Table B1B provides the tasks that the sponsor will examine to determine whether the FFS satisfactorily meets the requirements for flight crew training, testing, and experience, and provides the tasks for which the simulator may be qualified. (5) Table B1C provides the functions that an instructor/check pilot must be able to control in the simulator. (6) It is not required that all of the tasks that appear on the List of Qualified Tasks (part of the SOQ) be accomplished during the initial or continuing qualification evaluation.

Scenes must include a definable horizon and typical terrain characteristics such as fields, roads and bodies of water and surfaces illuminated by representative aircraft lighting (e.g., landing lights). Attachments to Chapter 4 Page 4-261 Attachment 4.2 – Guidance for planning Functions and Subjective Testing. Introduction (1) The following is an example test schedule for an Initial/Upgrade evaluation that covers the majority of the requirements set out in the Functions and Subjective test requirements (for Aeroplanes only). It is not intended that the schedule be followed line by line, rather, the example should be used as a guide for preparing a schedule that is tailored to the airplane or rotorcraft sponsor and training tasks. (2) Functions and subjective tests should be planned. This information has been organized as a reference document with the considerations, methods, and evaluation notes for each individual aspect of the simulator task presented as an individual item. In this way the evaluator can design his or her own test plan, using the appropriate sections to provide guidance on method and evaluation criteria. Two aspects should be present in any test plan structure: (a) An evaluation of the simulator to determine that it replicates the aircraft and performs reliably for an uninterrupted period equivalent to the length of a typical training session. (b) The simulator should be capable of operating reliably after the use of training device functions such as repositions or malfunctions. (3) A detailed understanding of the training task will naturally lead to a list of objectives that the simulator should meet. This list will form the basis of the test plan. Additionally, once the test plan has been formulated, the initial conditions and the evaluation criteria should be established. The evaluator should consider all factors that may have an influence on the characteristics observed during particular training tasks in order to make the test plan successful.

Chapter 5 – Type-specific flight training device (FTD) – qualification performance standards Overview Page 5-1 Chapter 5 Type-specific flight training device (FTD) - qualification performance standards 5.1 Overview (1) This chapter describes the qualification performance standards (QPS) for aeroplane and rotorcraft flight Training Devices (FTD) (Level 4 to Level 7). Whenever the term “aircraft” is used, it pertains to both aeroplanes and rotorcraft. The main body of Chapter 5 pertains to aircraft FSTDs. The technical requirements and evaluation criteria specific to aeroplane and rotorcraft FSTDs are presented in the following appendices and tables: A. Aeroplane FTD - QPS (a) Appendix C1 – Aeroplane FTD – General Simulator Requirements (b) Appendix C2 – Aeroplane FTD – Objective Test Requirements (c) Appendix C3 – Aeroplane FTD – Simulator Subjective Evaluations B. Rotorcraft FTD - QPS (a) Appendix D1 – Rotorcraft FTD – General Simulator Requirements (b) Appendix D2 – Rotorcraft FTD – Objective Test Requirements (c) Appendix D3 – Rotorcraft FTD – Simulator Subjective Evaluations Attachments: 5.2 General Description of Type-Specific Flight Training Device (1) Detailed standards and tests for the various levels of FTDs are fully defined in Appendices C1, C2 and C3 for aeroplanes and Appendices D1, D2 and D3 for rotorcraft. (a) Level 4 . A Level 4 FTD may have an open aircraft-specific flight deck area, or an enclosed aircraft-specific flight deck and at must have at least one operating system. Air/ground logic is required (no aerodynamic programming required). All displays may be flat/LCD panel representations or actual representations of displays in the aircraft. All controls, switches, and knobs may be touch sensitive activation (not capable of manual manipulation of the flight controls) or may physically replicate the aircraft in control operation. Note: Level 4 FTDs are qualified for procedural training only. If the FTD includes physical replication of primary flight controls and switches/knobs for automated flight control inputs (i.e. Flight control units / FMS), the Manager, Simulator Program (MSP) may recommend credit for specific training task, which may potentially reduce the required time in a Full Flight Simulator (FFS). Final approval for credits in an approved training program will rest solely with the Training Program Approval Authority (TPAA). The evaluation will consider the subjective performance of the aerodynamic flight model and whether the physical controls used in the training task fully support an effective pilot skill transfer to the FFS. Further Guidance is provided in at Section 5.10 FTD Level 4 – Subjective Evaluation Method. (b) Level 5 . A Level 5 FTD may have an open aircraft-specific flight deck area, or an enclosed aircraft-specific flight deck and a generic aerodynamic program. It must have at

Chapter 5 – Type-specific flight training device (FTD) – qualification performance standards Overview Page 5-2 least one operating system, and control loading representative of the simulated aircraft. The control loading need only represent the aircraft at approach speed and configuration. All displays may be flat/LCD panel representations or actual representations of displays in the aircraft. Primary and secondary flight controls (e.g. rudder; aileron; elevator; flaps; spoilers/speed brakes; engine controls; landing gear; nose-wheel steering; trim; brakes) must be physical controls. All other controls, switches, and knobs may be touch sensitive activation. (c) Level 6. A Level 6 device is one that has an enclosed aircraft-specific flight deck and aerodynamic program with all applicable aircraft systems operating and control loading that is representative of the simulated aircraft throughout its ground and flight envelope and significant sound representation. All displays may be flat/LCD panel representations or actual representations of displays in the aircraft, but all controls, switches, and knobs must physically replicate the aircraft in control operation. (d) Level 7. A level 7 FTD has an enclosed aircraft-specific flight deck and aerodynamic program with all applicable aircraft systems operating and control loading that is representative of the simulated aircraft throughout its ground and flight envelope and significant sound representation. All displays may be flat/LCD panel representations or actual representations of displays in the aircraft, but all controls, switches, and knobs must physically replicate the aircraft in control operation. Additional requirements are as follows: (e) Aeroplane FTDs must have a visual system that provides an out-of-the-flight deck view, providing cross-flight deck viewing (for both pilots simultaneously) of a field-of-view of at least: 180° horizontally and 40° vertically; (f) Rotorcraft FTDs must have a visual system that provides an out-of-the-flight deck view, providing cross-flight deck viewing (for both pilots simultaneously) of a field-of-view of at least: 146° horizontally and 36° vertically; and a vibration cueing system for characteristic rotorcraft vibrations noted at the pilot station(s). 5.3 Flight Test Validation Data (1) The requirements for gathering flight test data to validate FTD objective tests are the same as those for an FFS and can be found in Chapter 4, Section 4.2. The accuracy and resolution of the flight test data must be sufficient to clearly determine compliance with objective test criteria in Appendix C2, Table C2C for aeroplane FTDs or Appendix D2 Table D2C for rotorcraft FTDs. (2) Level 7 FTD objective tests must be validated using flight test data that has been gathered in accordance with a flight test program. (3) Level 6 FTD objective tests must be validated using flight test data that has been gathered in accordance with a flight test program. For Level 6 aeroplane FTDs, a sponsor may choose to use one or more of the alternative sources, procedures, and instrumentation described in Table C2C Note : Guidance and conditions for using the alternate sources for Level 6 aeroplane FTDs can be found in the preamble to Table C2C. (4) Level 5 FTD may be qualified based on generic aerodynamic programming that represents the set of aircraft in which the aircraft type simulated belongs. For rotorcraft FTDs and large aeroplanes FTDs (operating under CAR Part VI and VII), objective tests must be compared with flight test data that have been gathered in accordance with a flight test program. For small aeroplane FTDs (operating under CAR Part IV), the aerodynamic model and handling qualities may be validated using alternative data source and procedures found in Appendix C2, Table C2B – Level 5 FTD - Alternative Data Source for Small, Single and Multi-Engine Aeroplanes.

The MSP must be provided an opportunity to audit the use of the engineering simulation or the engineering simulator during the acquisition of the data that will be used as validation data. Engineering data may be used for changes that are incremental in nature. Manufacturers or other data suppliers must be able to demonstrate that the predicted changes in aircraft performance are based on acceptable aeronautical principles with proven success history and valid outcomes. This must include comparisons of predicted and flight test validated data. (2) The complete requirements for using engineering data are the same as those for a FFS and can be found in Chapter 4, Section 4.3. 5.5 Validation Test Tolerances - Non-Flight-Test Data (1) The objective-test tolerances listed in Appendix C2, Table C2A (aeroplanes) and Appendix D2, Table D2A (rotorcraft) provide a measureable means to compare and assess simulator performance against data acquired through actual flight-tests. Good engineering judgment should be applied to all tolerances in any test. A test fails when the results fall outside of the prescribed tolerance(s). (2) In some cases, engineering simulator data or other non-flight-test data sources may be considered if sound technical reasons or high costs prohibit the acquisition of flight-test data, or if alternative technical solutions are being proposed. If the use engineering data or non-flight-test data is allowed, then the data provider must supply a well-documented mathematical model and test procedure. (3) Engineering simulator data is deemed acceptable since the same simulation models used to generate the reference data are also used to test the FTD. The expected test results from both devices should therefore be very similar. For this reason, the expected tolerance for FTD objective tests validated using engineering data is reduced to 40% of those tolerances published in this manual for corresponding tests using flight-test data. However, there may be circumstances where the simulator models employed, or the manner in which they are integrated in the test loop, yield a higher fidelity than those supplied by the data provider. In these cases, it

Chapter 5 – Type-specific flight training device (FTD) – qualification performance standards Overview Page 5-4 is possible that an error greater than 40% may be acceptable if the sponsor can provide adequate explanation. The MSP may accept that the results from the two sources exceed 40% tolerance band based on justification relating to: (a) Hardware (avionics units and flight controls); (b) Iteration rates; (c) Execution order; (d) Integration methods; (e) Processor architecture; (f) Digital drift, including: (g) Interpolation methods; (h) Data handling differences; or (i) Auto-test trim tolerances. 5.6 Validation Data Roadmap (1) A Validation Data Roadmap (VDR) is a document that contains guidance material from the data supplier recommending the best possible sources of data to be used as validation data in the Qualification Test Guide (QTG). For Level 6 and 7 FTDS, aircraft manufacturers or other data suppliers must supply a VDR as part of the FSTD validation data package. A VDR is of special value when requesting an interim qualification, a qualification for simulators of aircrafts certificated prior to 1992, or an update qualification for alternate engine or avionics fits. A sponsor seeking to have an FSTD qualified in accordance with the QPS in this manual should submit a VDR to the MSP as early as possible in the planning stages. The MSP is the final authority to approve the data to be used as validation material in the QTG. (2) The VDR should identify (in matrix format) sources of data for all required objective tests. It should also provide guidance regarding the validity of these data for a specific engine type, thrust rating configuration, and the revision levels of all avionics affecting aircraft handling qualities and performance. The VDR should include rationale or explanation in test cases when; data or parameters are missing, engineering simulation data are to be used, flight test methods require explanation, or there are deviations from data requirements. Additionally, the document should refer to other appropriate sources of validation data (e.g., sound and vibration data documents). (3) A sample Validation Data Roadmap (VDR) is shown in Attachment 4.1 to Chapter 4. It depicts a generic roadmap matrix identifying sources of validation data for an abbreviated list of tests. A complete matrix should address all test conditions and provide actual data and data sources. 5.7 Acceptance Guidelines for Alternative Avionics (Flight-Related Computers and Controllers) (1) For a new aircraft type, the majority of flight validation data are collected on the first certified aircraft configuration with a “baseline” avionics ship-set. These data are then used to validate all flight simulators representing that aircraft type. Hardware design changes or software revisions to some baseline avionic systems, components or functionality may significantly alter the aircraft’s response, which in turn may significantly change the FTD performance and QTG results. Examples of such systems are; flight control computers, controllers for engines, autopilots, braking systems, nosewheel steering systems, and related avionics such as augmentation systems. (2) The MSP may require additional validation data for a FSTD with avionic hardware designs that differ from the baseline configuration, or if a software revision differs from a previously validated configuration. The QTG for a FSTD with additional or alternate avionics configurations should

Chapter 5 – Type-specific flight training device (FTD) – qualification performance standards Overview Page 5-5 contain selected objective test cases and data to validate any significant performance differences attributed to the avionics configuration. (3) Approval Guidelines for Validating Alternate Avionics. The MSP will apply the following guidelines when qualifying FSTDs representing aircrafts with a revised avionics configuration, or more than one avionics configuration: (a) The baseline validation data should be based on flight test data, except where other data are specifically allowed (e.g., engineering flight simulator data). (b) The sponsor is responsible for determining and disclosing whether validation data used in the QTG is affected by an alternative avionics fit. (c) Validation data from the previously validated avionics configuration may be used provided that: (i) Avionics system or component changes do not affect QTG results. This includes updates to avionics systems that are tied to aircraft response but do not affect QTG results (e.g., the avionics change is a Built-In-Test-Equipment (BITE) update or a modification in a different flight phase). The QTG should include authoritative justification from the aircraft manufacturer or system supplier that this avionics change does not affect the test; or (ii) No new functionality is added and the impact of the avionics change on the aircraft response is demonstrated to be small based on acceptable and proven aeronautical principles. This should be supplemented with avionics-specific validation data from the aircraft manufacturer's engineering simulation, using the revised avionics configuration. The QTG should include an explanation of the change and its effect on the aircraft response. (d) Supplemental flight test data is required to validate the alternate avionics revision if: (i) An avionics change significantly affects some QTG results, or (ii) New functionality is added to the avionics system. Note: Additional flight test validation data may not be needed if the avionics changes were certified without the need for testing with a comprehensive flight instrumentation package. The aircraft manufacturer should coordinate flight simulator data requirements in advance with the MSP. (e) The Validation Road Map in the QTG should be amended to reflect the appropriate validation data source for each test. The roadmap should identify the revision state of the avionics systems that could affect specific test responses. 5.8 Initial (and Upgrade) Qualification Requirements (1) In order to be qualified at a particular qualification level, the FTD must: (a) Meet the general requirements at Appendix C1 for aeroplanes, or Appendix D1 for rotorcrafts; (b) Meet the objective testing requirements at Appendix C2 for aeroplanes, or Appendix D2 for rotorcrafts; and (c) Satisfactorily accomplish the subjective tests at Appendix C3 for aeroplanes, or Appendix D3 for rotorcrafts. The items listed in the following tables are for simulator evaluation purposes only. They may not be used to limit or exceed the authorizations for use of a given level of simulator, as described on the SOQ, or as approved by the TPAA: (a) Tables A3A (Aeroplanes) and B3A (Rotorcraft) - Operations Tasks are tests that address pilot functions, including maneuvers and procedures (called flight tasks), and are divided by flight phases. The performance of these tasks by the MSP includes an operational examination of the visual system and special effects. There are flight tasks included to address some features of advanced technology aircrafts and innovative training programs. For example, “high angle-of-attack maneuvering” is included to provide a required alternative to “approach to stalls” for aircrafts employing flight envelope protection functions. (b) Tables A3A (Aeroplanes) and B3A (Rotorcraft), Operations Tasks; and Tables A3G and B3G, Instructor Operating Station are tests that address the overall function and control of the simulator including the various simulated environmental conditions; simulated aircraft system operations (normal, abnormal, and emergency); visual system displays; and special effects necessary to meet flight crew training, evaluation, or flight experience requirements. (2) All simulated aircraft systems functions will be assessed for normal and, where appropriate, alternate operations. Normal, abnormal, and emergency operations associated with a flight phase will be assessed during the evaluation of flight tasks or events within that flight phase. Simulated aircraft systems are listed separately under “Any Flight Phase” to ensure appropriate attention to systems checks. Operational navigation systems (including inertial navigation systems, global positioning systems, or other long-range systems) and the associated electronic

The NSEP evaluation report will identify any observed system operational discrepancies and any system limitation. (3) At the request of the TPAA, the MSP may assess a device to determine if it is capable of simulating certain training activities in a sponsor's training program, such as a portion of a Line Oriented Flight Training (LOFT) scenario. Unless directly related to a requirement for the qualification level, the results of such an evaluation would not affect the qualification level of the simulator. However, if the MSP determines that the simulator does not accurately simulate that training activity, the simulator would not be approved for that training activity. (4) Transport Canada intends to allow the use of Class III airport models when the sponsor provides the TPAA (or other regulatory authority) an appropriate analysis of the skills, knowledge, and proficiency objectives necessary for competent performance of the tasks using the Class III model. The analysis should describe the ability of the FTD/visual media and model to adequate support the required pilot training objective. The analysis should also include the specific media element, such as the airport model. 5.10 Flight Training Device Level 4 – Subjective Evaluation Method (1) A Level 4 FTD is one that may have an open aircraft-specific flight deck area, or an enclosed aircraft-specific flight deck and at least one operating system. The device must have air/ground logic but does not require an aerodynamic model validated against flight test data. All displays may be flat/LCD panel representations or actual representations of displays in the aircraft. All controls, switches, and knobs may be touch sensitive activation (not capable of manual manipulation of the flight controls) or may physically replicate the aircraft in control operation. Qualification of Level 4 FTDs are based on functions and subjective evaluation of the installed systems and their associated training tasks. (2) Level 4 FTDs are typically limited to procedural and system training only; however, some devices that physically replicate the aircraft in control operation and provide sophisticated avionic and aircraft system modelling, may allow training credits procedural training for certain tasks, which could potentially offset time required the FFS. In order to provide the TPAA with the guidance necessary to determine how the device could be used in an approved training program, the subjective evaluation must define the degree and range of training that each specific design can support. The NSEP has therefore adopted a method for subjective evaluation that allows the sponsor to identify the training tasks and the level of training that they propose for the Level 4 FTD qualification. The MSP will subjectively evaluate the device to determine whether the training tasks proposed are adequately supported and recommend an appropriate level of training for each task. Final approval for any credits in an approved training program will rest solely with the TPAA. (3) When responding to the sponsor’s letter of intent for evaluation (See Chapter 3), the MSP will provide a blank copy of Table C3E (aeroplanes) or Table D3E (Rotorcraft) to be completed by the sponsor prior to the evaluation. (a) The letter “N” has been pre-populated in Table C3E and D3E to denote tasks level assignments that are not appropriate for Level 4 FTDs or require validated aerodynamic and control models, or motion / visual cueing. (b) The sponsor may request tasks in addition to those listed in Table C3E and D3E. (c) The MSP will include a list of the task that have been assigned a training level on the FSTD certificate. This list will be the basis for subsequent recurrent evaluation. (4) The MSP will use the following criteria when assessing the level of training recommended for a particular task:

Chapter 5 – Type-specific flight training device (FTD) – qualification performance standards Overview Page 5-10 (a) Procedural Training. The FTD must sufficiently represent the system controls and functionality to train and rehearse procedures as per the type-specific AFM or SOP without modification or deviation. (b) Skill Training. The FTD must physically replicate all controls, knobs and switches used by the pilot to perform the task. The relative position of controls to the pilot seat position must be sufficiently representative to reinforce skill transfer to the FFS. The FTD must allow the pilot to apply procedures as per AFM or SOP without modification, deviation or instructor intervention. Avionic and aircraft system responses and behaviour must not interfere or distract from the task. (c) Manoeuvre Training. The FTD must meet the criteria for skill training for the specific task, and, the functionality and performance of the system or subsystems supporting the task must emulate the aircraft to a degree suitable for proficiency checks on the particular task. On a level 4 FTD, manoeuvre training credits are rare. They pertain only to systems or subsystems where the pilot proficiency is fully transferable to the FFS and will not require additional training in the FFS syllabus prior to a Pilot Proficiency Check (PPC). 5.11 Conduct of Initial and Upgrade Evaluations (1) The MSP will only evaluate those FTDs that are sponsored by a certificate holder as defined in Chapter 1 of this manual. However, the Minister may deem it appropriate to approve other FTD evaluations on a case-by-case basis provided they are conducted in accordance with applicable agreements. (2) The MSP will evaluate each FTD configuration as completely as possible. To ensure a thorough and uniform evaluation, each FTD will be evaluated against the general simulator requirements in Appendix C1 or D1, the objective tests listed in Appendix C2 (aeroplanes) or D2 (rotorcraft), and the subjective tests listed in Appendix C3 (aeroplanes) or D3 (rotorcraft), as applicable. The evaluations will include, but not necessarily be limited to the following: (a) Aircraft responses, including longitudinal and lateral-directional control responses (see Appendix C2 (aeroplanes) or D2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (b) Performance in authorized portions of the simulated aircraft's operating envelope, to include tasks evaluated by the MSP in the areas of surface operations, takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, approach, and landing as well as abnormal and emergency operations (see Appendix C2 (aeroplanes) or D2 (rotorcraft)); (c) Control checks (see Appendix C1 and C2 (aeroplanes) or Appendix D1 and D2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (d) Flight deck configuration (see Appendix C1 (aeroplanes) or D1 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (e) Pilot, flight engineer, and instructor station functions checks (see Appendix C1 and C3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix D1 and D3 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (f) Aircraft systems and sub-systems (as appropriate) as compared to the aircraft simulated (see Appendix C1 and C3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix D1 and D3 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (g) FTD systems and sub-systems, including force cueing (motion), visual, and aural (sound) systems, as appropriate (see Appendix C1 and C2 (aeroplanes) or Appendix D1 and D2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); and (h) Certain additional requirements, depending upon the qualification level sought, including equipment or circumstances that may become hazardous to the occupants. The sponsor may be subject to Occupational Safety and Health Administration requirements.

However, it is the sponsor’s responsibility to ensure TPAA approval for each air operator or private operator using the FTD in a TC approved training program. Note: For level 4 FTDs, the Qualification Certificate will include a list of the tasks from Table C3E that were subjectively evaluated and include the recommended training levels. (8) Under normal circumstances, the MSP will tentatively schedule a date for the initial or upgrade evaluation within fifteen (15) working days after receiving the sponsor’s request (letter of intent)

(5) During the continuing qualification evaluation conducted by the NSEP, the sponsor must also provide a person knowledgeable about the operation of the aircraft and the operation of the FTD. (6) The MSP will ensure the frequency of continuing qualification evaluations is in accordance with the requirements of section 606.03 of the Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs) unless the MSP becomes aware of discrepancies or performance problems with the device that warrants more frequent evaluations. (7) If the NSEP evaluator plans to accomplish specific tests during a normal continuing qualification evaluation that requires the use of special equipment or technicians, the sponsor will be notified as far in advance of the evaluation as practical; but not less than 72 hours. Examples of such tests include latencies, control dynamics, sounds and vibrations, motion, and/or some visual system tests. (8) The continuing qualification evaluations, described in Chapter 3, paragraph 3.8.3 of this manual will normally require 4 hours of FTD time. The sponsor should anticipate that some tests may require additional time. The continuing qualification evaluations will consist of the following: (a) Review of the results of the quarterly inspections conducted by the sponsor since the last scheduled continuing qualification evaluation. (b) A random selection of objective tests from the MQTG that provide an adequate opportunity to evaluate the performance of the FTD. The tests chosen will be performed either automatically or manually and should be able to be conducted within approximately one-third of the allotted FTD time.
