Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-1 Chapter 6 – Non-Type Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards 6.1 Overview (1) This chapter describes the qualification performance standards (QPS) for aeroplane and rotorcraft Flight Training Devices (FTD) (Level 1 and 2). Wherever the term “aircraft” is used, it refers to both aeroplanes and rotorcraft. The performance standards were derived from ICAO Document 9625 Edition 3 Volume 1 and 2, with some modifications based on an analysis of single and multi-engine; multi-crew coordination and Instrument Procedures Check requirements from and CAR Part IV training program requirements. The technical requirements and evaluation criteria specific to aeroplane and rotorcraft FSTDs are presented in the following appendices and tables: A. AEROPLANE - NON-TYPE SPECIFIC FTD - QPS (a) Appendix E1 – Aeroplane FTD – General Simulator Requirements (b) Appendix E2 – Aeroplane FTD – Objective Test Requirements (c) Appendix E3 – Aeroplane FTD – Simulator Subjective Evaluations B. ROTORCRAFT - NON-TYPE SPECIFIC FTD - QPS (a) Appendix F1 – Rotorcraft FTD – General Simulator Requirements (b) Appendix F2 – Rotorcraft FTD – Objective Test Requirements (c) Appendix F3 – Rotorcraft FTD – Simulator Subjective Evaluations ATTACHMENTS: (a) Attachment 6.1 - Sample FTD Certificate for Regional Authorities (b) Attachment 6.2 - Non-Type-Specific FTD Qualification Profile 6.2 Roles and Responsibilities (1) The NSEP is responsible for ensuring that all FSTDs used for pilot training and checking are evaluated in accordance with the requirements of CAR 606.03. To provide responsive and efficient service delivery and oversight, the MSP may delegate the conduct of initial evaluations of non-type-specific FTDs to Regional Authorities provided that: (a) The FTD product or series produced by a particular manufacturer has been previously approved in by the NSEP and operated in Canada; (b) The QTG does not present automated test results; (c) The sponsor is not requesting additional qualifications that are not covered by the QPS in this chapter. (2) The MSP may delegate recurrent evaluations of Level 1 and 2 FTDs to Regional Authorities after the NSEP completes the initial evaluation and follow-up corrective action. The Regional Authority may request the NSEP to participate in the first recurrent if knowledge transfer is required (particularly in the case of automatic testing). (3) The Regional Authority assuming oversight of a Level 1 or 2 FTD is responsible for: (a) verifying FTD sponsor eligibility; (b) conducting initial evaluations as delegated;

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-2 (c) conducting recurrent evaluations in accordance with CAR 606.03; (d) tracking and ensuring corrective action of discrepancies noted during the evaluations; (e) Issue certificate: (f) TCID number, (g) FTD Sponsor, (h) FTD location, (i) manufacturer/model, (j) aircraft class/set simulated, (k) serial number, (l) issuing authority (Region) (m) FTD Level and special qualifications, (n) QPS used (o) Date of issue and expiry date. (p) Qualification Profile (as page 2). (4) Maintaining a record of FTD certificates, TCID numbers issued; evaluation reports and associated qualification documents. Note: Sample certificate and qualification profile form is shown at attachments 6.1 and 6.2 (RDIMS #13698343). Note: TCID numbers issued by Regional Authorities are 4 digits, where the first digit represents the Region as follows: Atlantic Region – 2xxx; Quebec Region - 3xxx; Ontario Region - 4xxx; Prairie Northern Region – 5xxx; Pacific Region – 6xxx. TCID numbers 0 to 1999 are reserved for NSEP use. 6.3 General Description of Non-Type-Specific FTDs (1) Unlike type-specific FTDs, non-type-specific FTDs are intended to be representative of a class or set of aircrafts. The expression “generic device” has traditionally been used to designate such non-type-specific devices; however, in this chapter, the expression “generic device” has been replaced by “non-type-specific” to preclude confusion with the simulation feature fidelity as defined by the Table 6.2-1 below. Note : Class” in relation to the classification of aircrafts, means aircrafts having similar operating characteristics to single-engine aircrafts, multi-engine aircrafts, centre-line thrust aircrafts, land aircrafts or sea aircrafts. Note: Set of Aircraft” is a group or series of aircraft group that share similar handling and operating characteristics, similar operating envelopes, and have the same number and type of engines or power- plants. Fidelity Aircraft simulation Sound, Motion and Visual Cueing Environment simulation Generic Not specific to aircraft model, type or variant. Generic to an aircraft of its class. Simple modelling of key basic cueing features. For visual cueing only: Generic visual environment with perspective Simple modelling of key basic environment features.

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-3 Fidelity Aircraft simulation Sound, Motion and Visual Cueing Environment simulation sufficient to support basic instrument flying and transition to visual from straight in instrument approaches. Representative Representative of an aircraft of its class, e.g., to engine turbo-prop aircraft. It does not have to be type specific. For sound and motion cueing only: Replicates a specific aircraft in set of aircrafts to the maximum extent possible. For visual cueing only: Representative of the real world visual environment and perspective. Representative of the real world environment. Specific Replicates the specific aeroplane model, type or variant. Applicable to visual cueing only: replicates the real world visual environment and (infinity) perspective. Replicates the real world environment as far as possible for any specific location. 6.4 Type-Specific FTD Levels (1) The Non-Type-Specific FTD levels were developed to provide guidance and minimum FTD requirements to Flight Training Units (FTUs) who seek approval to use a lower cost FTDs in approved training programs for single and multi-engine licensing, multi crew coordination (MCC) (for aeroplanes only), and Instrument Proficiency Checks (IPC) (for aeroplanes only). These devices are not authorized for any experience, training or checking credits in type-specific approved training programs. MCC and IPC training or checking on FTDs simulating aeroplanes that require a type-rating may only be conducted on type-specific FTDs (See para 6.4.3 for eligible FTDs) (2) There are two basic non-type-specific FTD configuration: (a) Level 1 - A level 1 FTD is the lowest fidelity device and may have a “generic” cockpit design. The device does not require a visual system or active force-feedback flight controls. It will support basic instrument procedural training, and may provide experience credit for 5 hours pursuant to CAR 421.26(4)(a) pending evaluation. (b) Level 2 – A Level 2 FTD, is a device that represents a “designated” class and set of aircraft. The device requires active force-feedback flight controls and requires a visual system that meets the minimum requirements in Tables E1A or F1A as applicable. It will support basic instrument procedure training and may provide experience credit for 10 hours pursuant to CAR 421.30(4)(a)(ii)(A)(III) pending evaluation. (3) An aeroplane FTD may qualify for instrument proficiency checks (IPC) and/or for multi-crew coordination (MCC) training in an ATP(A) program if the device meets the following criteria. (a) MCC Qualification. An FTD may qualify as a Multi-Crew Coordination FTD provided that it: (i) Meets the criteria objective and subjective test criteria for an FTD Level 2, 5, 6, or 7; and

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-4 (ii) Meets or exceeds the criteria outlined in Appendices E for the MCC qualification; and (iii) Fully supports the procedural and operational performance tasks required in the TC approved training program for ATP(A), per CAR as amended. (4) IPC Qualification. An FTD will qualify as a platform to conduct Instrument Proficiency Checks (IPC) provided that it: (a) Meets the criteria objective and subjective test criteria for an FTD Level 2, 5, 6, or 7; (b) Meets or exceeds the criteria outlined in Appendices E for the IPC qualification; and (c) Fully supports the procedural and operational performance tasks IPC in the Advisory Circular AC-401-004 as amended to conduct an IPC. Note: An aeroplane FTD granted an additional MCC or IPC qualification will be designated on the FSTD certificate as Level #-MCC. (i.e. Level 5-MCC; Level 2-IPC; Level 6-MCC/IPC) Note: The term “Designated” is used when a feature or requirement must be specifically identified by the sponsor prior to the initial evaluation or update evaluation. (5) Detailed standards and tests for the various levels of FTDs are fully defined in Appendices E for aeroplanes and Appendices F for rotorcraft. 6.5 General Design Standards (1) To avoid any delays in the design, build, acceptance, or qualification process, the sponsor should engage in early discussions with the TPAA and Approving Authority to broadly agree on the “designated aircraft configuration” and any additional qualifications (MCC or IPC) intended. (2) Cockpit/Flight Deck Configuration. The Sponsor should choose a configuration that sensibly represents the aircrafts likely to be used in the approved training program. To ensure a good training environment, the cockpit/flight deck should be located in a training environment that minimizes any distractions. (a) Level 1. The cockpit/flight deck must sufficiently represent a class of aircraft to support approved use. The cockpit/flight deck may be open or enclosed. The appearance, arrangement, operation, and function of physical switches and other required controls must be realistically placed. The instrument panel of an aeroplane FTD must include at least the following: (i) Master/battery; (ii) Magnetos for each engine (as applicable); (iii) Alternators for each engine; (iv) Fuel boost pumps for each engine; (v) Avionics master; (vi) Pitot heat; and (vii) Rotating beacon/strobe, navigation, taxi, and landing lights. (b) Level 2. The cockpit/flight deck must be representative of a set of aircrafts or the aircraft itself to support approved use. The cockpit/flight deck must be sufficiently enclosed to minimize distractions. The physical arrangement, appearance, and operation of controls, instruments, and switches should model at least one aircraft in the family of aircraft represented as closely as practicable.

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-5 (3) Cockpit/Flight Deck Components. Physical flight and aircraft system controls must be recognizable as to their function and how they are to be manipulated solely from their appearance. (a) Physical flight and aircraft system controls must not use interfaces such as a keyboard, mouse, or gaming joystick to control the represented aircraft in simulated flight. (b) Components used within the cockpit/flight deck area do not need to be aircraft parts; however, any parts used should be representative of typical training aircrafts and should be robust enough to endure the training tasks. (c) The use of simple flat display technology-based representations and touch-screen controls to represent objects other than basic push-button types of controls will not be acceptable. The training tasks envisaged for these devices are such that appropriate layout and feel is very important. For example, the altimeter sub-scale knob needs to be physically located on the altimeter. The use of flat display technologies with physical overlays incorporating operational switches/knobs/ buttons replicating an aircraft instrument panel may be acceptable. 6.6 Data package (1) The data for the aerodynamics model, flight controls and engines used in Level 1 or 2 FTDs must be based on sound engineering principles and substantiated in the form of a “Reference Data” engineering report (RDR). The RDR shall show that the proposed validation data are representative of the aircraft or the class of aircrafts modelled. This report may include flight test data, manufacturer’s design data, information from the aircraft flight manual (AFM) and maintenance manuals, results of approved or commonly accepted simulations or predictive models, recognized theoretical results, information from the public domain, or other sources as deemed necessary by the FTD manufacturer to substantiate the proposed model. (2) Generic or representative data may be derived from a specific aircraft within the class of aircrafts simulated, or it may be based on information from several aircrafts within a group of aircrafts that reflect the performance of the “designated aircraft configuration”. (3) With the concurrence of the NSEP, the data may be in the form of a manufacturer’s previously approved set of validation data for the applicable FTD. The sponsor should submit the intended validation data together with a substantiation report to the NSEP for review and approval prior to procurement or the commencement of the manufacturing or procurement process. Once the set of data for a specific FTD has been accepted and approved by the NSEP, it will become the validation data that will be used as reference for subsequent recurrent evaluations with the application of the stated tolerances. (4) Data Collection and Model Development . A basic requirement for any modelling is the integrity of the mathematical equations and models used to represent the flying qualities and performance of the aircraft or class of aircrafts being simulated. The models should be continuous and vary sensibly throughout the required training flight envelope. The following principles apply: (a) Additional data to refine the non-type-specific model can be obtained from many sources, such as aircraft design data, flight and maintenance manuals, observations on the ground and in the air, etc., without necessarily having to conduct expensive, dedicated flight testing. (b) Data obtained on the ground and in flight can be measured and recorded using a range of simple means such as video cameras, paper and pencil, stopwatch, and new technologies (e.g. GPS). (c) Data gathering should take place at representative masses and centres of gravity. Development of such a data package including justification and the rationale for the design and intended performance, the measurement methods and recorded parameters

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-6 (e.g. mass, CG, atmospheric conditions) should be carefully documented and available for inspection by the NSEP as part of the qualification process. (5) Flight Controls. There can be a strong interaction between the flight control forces and the effects of both the engines and the aerodynamic configuration and will reflect the fidelity and credits offered to the FTD: (a) Level 1 FTDs only require “generic” fidelity level flight controls, which may be achieved with a passive force cueing system utilizing springs. The evaluator will assess the fidelity of the flight controls during the initial and recurrent evaluations. Qualification will not be awarded if the flight controls manifest any characteristics that would result in negative training. (b) Level 2 FTDs require “representative” fidelity level flight controls, which will require an active force feedback cueing system that allows flight controls forces to vary with position as well as aircraft configuration (speed, flaps, trim). 6.7 Visual System (1) The adequacy of the performance of the visual system will be determined by its ability to support the intended training tasks, e.g. “visual cueing sufficient to support changes in approach path by using runway perspective”. (2) Collimated visual optics are not required for non-type-specific FTDs since no training credits for landing are available. A single channel direct viewing system is acceptable for level 2. For MCC and IPC additional qualifications, the visual FOV must be as per Appendix E2 (applicable to aeroplanes FTDs only). (3) Where the device does not simulate a particular aircraft type, the design of the out-of- cockpit/flight deck view should be matched to the visual system so that the pilot has a FOV sufficient for the intended training tasks. For example, during an instrument approach the pilot should be able to see the appropriate visual segment at decision height. Additionally, where the aircraft deviates from the normal approach path, undue loss of visual reference should not occur during the subsequent correction. 6.8 Transport Delay (1) For a non-type-specific device, a transport delay test may be used to demonstrate that the FSTD system does not exceed the permissible delay. However, for such a device using simple models, a Statement of Compliance (SOC) may be acceptable in lieu of a test. The SOC must contain a system block diagram that support a description of the cumulative latency or transport delay from control input to instrument, visual and motion system response as applicable. The SOC should also describe the method of determining the transport delay. (2) The maximum permissible transport delays is 300 milliseconds for aeroplanes and 120 milliseconds for rotorcraft. A test may be required during the initial evaluation to verify the SOC if the calculated transport delay is close to the maximum permissible value. 6.9 Testing/Evaluation (1) To ensure that any device meets its design criteria initially and periodically throughout its life, a system of objective and subjective testing will be used. (2) The validation tests specified in Appendix E2 for aeroplanes and Appendix F2 for rotorcrafts will be flown by a suitably skilled person and the results recorded manually. (3) Automatic Recording and Testing. The MSP must be notified if a sponsor wishes to use automatic recording and testing for validation tests. In such a case, the QTG review will be

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-7 conducted by the NSEP. Based on the complexity of the QTG and the results of the QTG review, the MSP will decide whether it is appropriate to retain NSEP oversight of the device or to delegate oversight to the Regional Authority. (4) The tolerances specified are designed to ensure that the device meets its original target criteria year after year. It is therefore important that such target data are carefully derived and values are accepted by the NSEP or Regional Authority in advance of the initial evaluation (QTG review). Unlike the target parameters stipulated for type-specific devices, those stated for non-type-specific FSTDs are primarily intended to ensure repeatability during the life of the FSTD and in particular at each recurrent regulatory inspection. For initial qualification, the device should meet its design criteria within the listed tolerances; however, the evaluator may approve reasonably altered target values if they do not adversely affect the performance of the FTD or the quality of training and the results are repeatable. (5) A number of tests within the QTG have had their tolerances reduced to “Correct Trend and Magnitude” (CT&M) thereby avoiding the need for specific validation data. The use of CT&M is not to be taken as an indication that certain areas of simulation can be ignored. For such tests, the performance of the FSTD should be appropriate and representative of the simulated aircraft and should under no circumstances exhibit negative characteristics. Where CT&M is used as a tolerance, it is strongly recommended that a simple, reliable, and repeatable test method be designed to establish a baseline result approved during the initial evaluation. This will be provide a means of avoid or resolving any divergent subjective opinions during recurrent evaluations. (6) Longitudinal change force tests . For Level 1 and 2 aeroplane FTDs, it is acceptable to use change force tests instead of the longitudinal power, flap and gear change dynamics tests. The purpose of these change force tests is to simply reproduce the control force feeling during recurrent evaluations. These tests should be conducted in the following way: (a) Trim the aeroplane in straight and level flight in the most suitable configuration; (b) Initiate the configuration change (power, flap or gear change); (c) Maintain the airspeed constant using the pitch control (or as an alternate procedure, maintain the altitude of the original trimmed conditions); and (d) Measure the required pitch control force change. Note: If automatic testing is used, a change dynamics test is acceptable. (7) The subjective tests listed in Appendix E (aeroplanes) and F (rotorcraft) must be flown by a suitably qualified and experienced pilot. 6.10 Initial and Upgrade) Qualification Requirements (1) In order to be qualified at a particular qualification level, the FTD must: (a) Meet the general requirements at Appendix E1 for aeroplanes, or Appendix F1 for rotorcrafts; (b) Meet the objective testing requirements at Appendix E2 for aeroplanes, or Appendix F2 for rotorcrafts; and (c) Satisfactorily accomplish the subjective tests at Appendix E3 for aeroplanes, or Appendix F3 for rotorcrafts. (2) Sponsors applying for an initial evaluation must follow the procedures at Section 6.11 of this chapter. The evaluating agency must be in receipt of the following prior to conducting an evaluation: (a) A statement that the FTD meets all provisions of the QPS. The Sponsor’s application must also:

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-8 (i) identify the class, set of aircraft or aircraft type simulated and any additional qualifications requested (i.e. IPC or MCC): and (ii) Designate airport navigation and visual scenes, and operational systems as required by the QPS for the level and additional qualifications requested. (b) Unless otherwise authorized, the sponsor must send a letter of compliance to the MSP or Regional Authority (as described in paragraph 6.11.1c of this chapter) no later than 5 business days prior to the scheduled. (c) A QTG, acceptable to the MSP, that includes all of the following where required by the QPS: (i) Objective data obtained from aircraft testing or another approved source. (ii) Objective test results obtained from the performance of the FTD. (iii) Result of FTD subjective tests. (iv) A description of the equipment necessary to perform the evaluation for initial qualification and the continuing qualification evaluations. (d) Unless otherwise approved by the MSP, the sponsor’s QTG submission must include results of all required tests conducted at the sponsor's training facility after the FTD is assembled with systems and sub-systems functional and operating in an interactive manner. (3) During the initial (or upgrade) qualification evaluation, the sponsor must provide a person to assist with the evaluation who is a user of the device (e.g., a qualified pilot or instructor pilot with flight time experience in that aircraft) and knowledgeable about the operation of the aircraft and the FTD. 6.11 Application for initial or Upgrade Evaluations (1) The application process for an initial or upgrade qualification evaluation for a non-type-specific FTD will be administered according to the following steps: (a) Letter of Intent. For each FSTD, the sponsor must submit a “letter of intent” requesting an initial qualification evaluation to their Regional Authority no later than 120 days prior to the evaluation date requested. The letter will include: (i) A description of the FSTD; (ii) The anticipated qualification level of the FSTD; (iii) The make, model, and series of aircraft simulated; and any other pertinent information; and (iv) Any additional information that may affect the scope of the evaluation (i.e. FSTD relocation, sponsorship change, restoration after voluntary suspension etc.) Note: To avoid any qualification delays, the sponsor should contact the MSP as early as possible to coordinate a review and acceptance of the validation data package. (2) Regional Authority’s Response . The Regional Authority will liaise with the MSP to determine the most appropriate evaluation agency (NSEP or Regional Authority). The designated evaluating agency will reply to the letter of intent within 15 business days with the following information; (a) Tentative dates for the initial evaluation; (b) The date the sponsor must submit the QTG if applicable;

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-9 (c) An attached “qualification profile” form to be completed and returned with the QTG submission. (d) Any special equipment and qualified personnel needed to accomplish or assist in the accomplishment of tests during initial qualification. (3) QTG Review. The Sponsor will submit the QTG and the Reference Data Report (RDR) in a form and manner described in this chapter. The evaluating agency will review the QTG and forward comments and questions resulting from the review to the Sponsor for their response. Depending on the results of the review, the designated evaluating agency will confirm or postpone the evaluation date. The sponsor will provide a response to the QTG review comments no later than 5 working days before the evaluation date. (4) Letter of Compliance. The Sponsor will submit a “letter of compliance” signed by the management representative no later than 5 working days before the evaluation confirming that: (a) Qualified pilot(s), after having flown all of the applicable subjective evaluation in the applicable QPS appendix tests (Table E1B for aeroplane FTDs) relevant to the qualification level of the FSTD, have determined that the performance and handling qualities of the FTD represent those of the class or set of aircraft within the normal operating envelope. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. The name of the pilot(s) making this determination must be identified on the letter of compliance. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. (b) Qualified pilot(s) or person(s) trained on simulator systems/sub-systems and trained on the operation of the simulated aircraft systems, after having exercised the operation of the FTD and the pertinent functions available through the Instructor Operating Station(s), have determined that the FTD cockpit configuration, systems, and sub-systems (including the simulated aircraft systems) functionally represent those in the aircraft class or set of aircraft. The name of the person(s) making this determination must be available to the MSP upon request. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. (c) When the FSTD passes an evaluation for initial qualification, the MSP issues a Qualification Certificate as described at paragraph 6.2.3 of this chapter. (5) After the NSEP completes the evaluation for initial qualification, the sponsor must update the Qualification Test Guide (QTG), with the results of the TC-witnessed tests as determined by the evaluator. (6) Upon issuance of the Qualification Certificate the updated QTG becomes the Master Qualification Test Guide (MQTG). The MQTG must be made available to the Regional Authority or NSEP upon request. 6.12 Qualification Test Guide (QTG) (1) The sponsor must submit the QTG to the NSEP or delegated Regional Authority for review and approval, and must include: (a) A QTG cover page with sponsor and TC approval signature blocks; (b) An FTD information page that provides the information listed in this. For convertible FTDs, the sponsor must submit a separate page for each configuration of the FTD; (i) The sponsor's FTD identification number or code. (ii) The aircraft model and series being simulated. (iii) The reference to the data record document. (iv) The source of the basic aerodynamic model and the aerodynamic coefficient data used to modify the basic model.

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-10 (v) The engine model(s) (class) (vi) The flight control configuration (reference aircraft model). (vii) The flight management system identification and revision level. (viii) The FTD model and manufacturer. (ix) The date of FTD manufacture. (x) The FTD computer identification. (xi) The visual system model and manufacturer, including display type. (xii) The motion system type and manufacturer, including degrees of freedom. (2) A Table of Contents. (a) A log of revisions and a list of effective pages. (b) List of all relevant data references. (c) A glossary of terms and symbols used (including sign conventions and units). (d) Statements of compliance and capability (SOCs) as required by the QPS. (e) Recording procedures or equipment required to accomplish the objective tests if applicable. (f) The following information for each objective test required in Appendix E2, Table E2A (aeroplanes) or Appendix F2, Table F2A (rotorcraft) as applicable: (g) Name of the test. (h) Objective of the test. (i) Tolerances parameters and flight conditions. (j) Pertinent and complete Manual test procedures. (Including a list of all relevant parameters driven or constrained during the manually test setup). (k) A means of comparing the FTD test results to the reference data or targets. (l) Other information as necessary, to assist in the evaluation or interpretation of the test results. (3) For FTDs using Auto-testing utilities , the following information in addition to para i (above) must be included for each objective test: (a) Initial conditions. (b) Automatic test procedures (if applicable). (c) Method for evaluating FTD objective test results. (d) A list of all relevant parameters driven or constrained during the automatically conducted test(s). (e) Tolerances for relevant parameters. (f) Source of Validation Data (document and page number). (g) Copy of the Validation Data (if located in a separate binder, a cross reference for the identification and page number for pertinent data location must be provided). (h) Simulator Objective Test Results as obtained by the sponsor. Each test result must reflect the date completed and must be clearly labeled as a product of the device being tested.

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-11 (4) TC considers convertible FTDs as a separate FTD for each converted configuration. If a sponsor seeks qualification for two or more models of an aircraft type using a convertible FTD, the sponsor must submit a QTG for each aircraft model, or a QTG for the first aircraft model and a supplement to that QTG for each additional aircraft model. The evaluating agency will conduct a separate evaluation on each aircraft model and issue the sponsor a separate TCID / certificate for each model that satisfactorily meets evaluation criteria. (5) The following describes the acceptable form and manner of presentation of objective test results in the QTG: (a) The sponsor's FTD test results must be recorded and presented in a manner that allows easy comparison of the FTD test results to the validation data or targets. (b) Tests results must be labeled using terminology common to aircraft parameters as opposed to computer software identifications. (c) Validation data documents included in a QTG may be photographically reduced only if such reduction will not alter the graphic scaling or cause difficulties in scale interpretation or resolution. (d) Scaling on graphical presentations must provide the resolution necessary to evaluate the parameters shown in Appendix E2, Table E2A for aeroplanes, or Appendix F2, Table F2A for rotorcrafts. (e) For auto-tests that involve time histories, data sheets (or transparencies thereof) and FTD test results must be clearly marked with appropriate reference points to ensure an accurate comparison between the FTD and the aircraft with respect to time. Time histories recorded via a line printer are to be clearly identified for cross plotting on the aircraft data. Over-plots must not obscure the reference data. (6) The sponsor must maintain a copy of the MQTG at the FTD location. Note: A sample QTG for Level 1 and 2 FTDs can be found in TP13799 - Qualification Test Guide – CAR Part IV Flight Training Devices. 6.13 Notification of FTD Modifications and updates (1) The sponsor must notify the Regional Authority in writing at least 21 days prior to making a modification to a non-type-specific FTD. For the purposes of this manual, an FSTD is said to have been modified when: (a) Equipment or devices intended to simulate aircraft appliances are added to or removed from the FSTD, which change the MQTG or the Qualification Certificate issued by the Minister; or (b) Changes are made to either software or hardware that; (i) are intended to impact flight or ground dynamics; (ii) that impact performance or handling characteristics of the FSTD (including motion, visual, control loading, or sound systems for those FSTD levels requiring sound tests and measurements); or (iii) require an amendment to the MQTG. Note: Routine software or hardware changes, or changes to the MQTG which do not affect required objective testing results or validation data approved during the initial evaluation of the FSTD are not considered modifications. (2) Notification and approval process . The notification and approval process for an update or modification is as follows:

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-12 (a) Letter of Intent. For each FTD, the sponsor will submit a “letter of intent” to the Regional Authority that: i) Provides a description of the modification or update; ii) Identifies any procedural, functional or physical change to the FSTD that may affect pilot training and checking; iii) Identifies impact flight or ground dynamics; changes are made that impact performance or handling characteristics of the FTD; iv) Identifies any required changes to the MQTG; and v) Provides a date when the modification or update would be available for evaluation. (b) Regional Authority Response . The regional office will reply to the letter of intent within 5 business days with the following; i) Whether an update evaluation is required, ii) Tentative date and scope of the update evaluation if required, iii) Any special equipment and qualified personnel needed to accomplish or assist in the accomplishment of tests during the update evaluation, and iv) Any additional requirements for approval if an update evaluation is deemed unnecessary. Note: Depending on the complexity and impact on training, the MSP may approve a modification based on a letter of compliance from the sponsor. (c) Letter of Compliance. The Sponsor will submit a “letter of compliance” signed by the management representative no later than 5 working days before a modification is implemented or evaluated confirming that: (i) Qualified pilot(s), after having flown the FTD, have determined that the performance and handling qualities represent those of the class or set of aircraft within the normal operating envelope. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. The name of the pilot(s) making this determination must be identified on the letter of compliance. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. (ii) Qualified pilot(s) or person(s) trained on simulator systems/sub-systems and trained on the operation of the simulated aircraft systems, after having exercised the operation of the FTD and the affected functions through the Instructor Operating Station(s), have determined that all affected systems, and sub- systems (including the simulated aircraft systems) functionally represent those in the aircraft class or set of aircraft. The name of the person(s) making this determination must be available to the MSP upon request. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. (3) Approval. The Regional Authority will approve the use of a modification when: (a) The FTD successfully passes a special evaluation; or (b) The Regional Authority has notified the sponsor that the letter of compliance has been accepted in lieu of an evaluation.; and (c) The Qualification Certificate has been appropriately amended to reflect any changes to the FTD.

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-13 6.14 Conduct of Initial and Update Evaluation (1) The Regional Authority may only evaluate non-type-specific FTDs for sponsors holding a TC certificate as a Flight Training Unit. The NSEP will evaluate all type-specific FTDs. (2) The evaluator will assess each FTD configuration as completely as possible. To ensure a thorough and uniform evaluation, each FTD will be evaluated against the general simulator requirements in Appendix E1 or F1, the objective tests listed in Appendix E2 (aeroplanes) or F2 (rotorcraft), and the subjective tests listed in Appendix E3 (aeroplanes) or F3 (rotorcraft), as applicable. The evaluations will include, but not necessarily be limited to the following: (a) Aircraft responses, including longitudinal and lateral-directional control responses (see Appendix E2 (aeroplanes) or F2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (b) Performance in authorized portions of the simulated aircraft's operating envelope, to include tasks evaluated by the MSP in the areas of surface operations, takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, approach, and landing as well as abnormal and emergency operations (see Appendix E2 (aeroplanes) or F2 (rotorcraft)); (c) Control checks (see Appendix E1 and E2 (aeroplanes) or Appendix F1 and F2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (d) Flight deck configuration (see Appendix E1 (aeroplanes) or F1 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (e) Pilot, flight engineer, and instructor station functions checks (see Appendix E1 and E3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix F1 and F3 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (f) Aircraft systems and sub-systems (as appropriate) as compared to the aircraft simulated (see Appendix E1 and E3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix F1 and F3 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (g) FTD systems and sub-systems, including force cueing (motion), visual, and aural (sound) systems, as appropriate (see Appendix E1 and F2 (aeroplanes) or Appendix E1 and F2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); and (h) Certain additional requirements, depending upon the qualification level sought, including equipment or circumstances that may become hazardous to the occupants. The sponsor may be subject to Occupational Safety and Health Administration requirements. (3) The evaluator will administers the objective and subjective tests, which includes an examination of functions. The tests include a qualitative assessment of the FTD by a TC pilot. (a) Objective tests provide a basis for measuring and evaluating FTD performance and determining compliance with the requirements of this chapter. (b) Subjective tests provide a basis for: (i) Evaluating the capability of the FTD to perform over a typical utilization period; (ii) Determining that the FTD satisfactorily simulates each required task; (iii) Verifying correct operation of the FTD controls, instruments, and systems; and (iv) Demonstrating compliance with the requirements of this manual. (4) In addition to the scheduled continuing qualification evaluation, each FTD is subject to evaluations conducted by the NSEP or Regional Authority at any time without prior notification to the sponsor. Such evaluations would be accomplished in a normal manner (i.e. requiring exclusive use of the FTD for the conduct of objective and subjective tests and an examination of functions) if the FTD is not being used for pilot training and checking. However, if the FTD were being used, the evaluation would be conducted in a non-exclusive manner. The FTD evaluator will accompany the instructor aboard the FTD along with the student(s) and observe the operation of the FTD during the training, testing, or checking activities in a non-interference manner.

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-14 (5) If it is determined that the results of an objective test do not support the level requested but do support a lower level, the Regional Authority may qualify the FTD at that lower level or remove an additional qualification to permit the device to enter into training. (6) After an FTD is evaluated and deemed compliant, the Regional Authority issues a Qualification Certificate to the sponsor. The Certificate is also the Regional Authority’s recommendation to the TPAA that the FTD may be used in a TC approved training program. (7) The numbering system used for objective test results in the QTG should closely follow the numbering system set out in Appendix E2, Table E2A (aeroplanes) or Appendix F2, Table F2A (rotorcraft) as applicable. 6.15 Continuing Qualification Evaluations and Requirements (1) The sponsor must conduct objective tests at least once annually and retain test results and the FTD defect log for at least two consecutive years. (2) During the continuing qualification evaluation conducted by the Regional Authority, the sponsor must also provide a person knowledgeable about the operation of the aircraft and the operation of the FTD. (3) The Regional Authority will ensure the frequency of continuing qualification evaluations is in accordance with the requirements of CAR 606.03 unless the Regional Authority becomes aware of discrepancies or performance problems with the device that warrants more frequent evaluations. (4) The continuing qualification evaluations will normally require 4 hours of FTD time. The sponsor should anticipate that evaluations will consist of the following: (a) Review of the sponsor-conducted objective tests results and defect log. (b) A random selection of objective tests from the MQTG that provide an adequate opportunity to evaluate the performance of the FTD. The tests chosen will be performed manually and should be able to be conducted within approximately one-third of the allotted FTD time. (c) A subjective evaluation of the FTD to perform a representative sampling of the tasks set out in Appendix E3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix F3 (rotorcraft) as applicable. This portion of the evaluation should take approximately two-thirds of the allotted FTD time. (d) An examination of the functions of the FTD may include the motion system, visual system, sound system, instructor operating station, and the normal functions and simulated malfunctions of the aircraft systems. This examination is normally accomplished simultaneously with the subjective evaluation requirements.

Appendix E2 – Aeroplane Non-Type Specific FTD – Objective Tests Page 6-56 Appendix E2 - Aeroplane Non-Type-Specific FTD – Objective Tests (1) In addition to subjective testing, non-type-specific FTDs will be subject to the applicable objective tests at Table E2A to ensure the they meet qualification criteria initially and periodically throughout its life. The objective tests can be flown by a suitably skilled person and the results recorded manually. (2) The tolerances specified are designed to ensure that the device meets its original target criteria year after year. It is therefore important that such target data is carefully derived and substantiated prior to submitting the QTG to the inspecting authority prior to the QTG review and initial qualification. For initial qualification, it is highly desirable that the device should meet its design criteria within the listed tolerances. However, unlike the tolerances stipulated for type- specific devices, the tolerances stated for non-type-specific FSTDs are intended to support recurrent inspection to ensure the device is maintained as approved during the initial evaluation. It is therefore important that the tests targets be representative and test results be repeatable during the life of the FSTD. (3) A number of tests within the QTG have had their tolerances reduced to "Correct Trend and Magnitude" (CT&M) thereby avoiding the need for specific validation data. The use of CT&M is not to be taken as an indication that certain areas of simulation can be ignored. For such tests, the performance of the FSTD should be appropriate and representative of the simulated designated aeroplane and should under no circumstances exhibit negative characteristics. Where CT&M is used as a tolerance, it is strongly recommended that targets are identified and used to footprint the baseline in order to avoid possible divergent subjective opinions during recurrent evaluations. Once a footprint target is established, then the applicable tolerance should be applied to results during recurrent evaluations. (4) Longitudinal change force tests. It is acceptable to use change force tests instead of the longitudinal power, flap and gear change dynamics tests. The purpose of these change force tests is to simply reproduce the control force feeling during recurrent evaluations. If not otherwise stated, these tests should be conducted in the following way: (a) trim the aeroplane in straight and level flight in the most suitable configuration; (b) initiate the configuration change (power, flap or gear change); (c) maintain the airspeed constant using the pitch control (or as an alternate procedure, maintain the altitude of the original trimmed conditions); and (d) Measure the required pitch control force change. Note: If change forces are small (within the tolerance band), it is acceptable to reduce change the end state airspeed to achieve a more measureable force provided the procedure is well documented and repeatable.

Handling Qualities Note 1: Pitch, roll, yaw and collective controller position versus force or time should be measured at the control using external test fixtures. An alternative method using recording and measuring instrumentation built into the FSTD is acceptable provided that the sponsor verifies the force and position data from this instrumentation matches the helicopter data by using external measuring equipment while conducting the static control checks, or equivalent means. The verification test must be conducted on-site prior to the initial evaluation and the results of the comparison must be included in the MQTG. If the results are satisfactory, the instrumentation may be used during initial and recurrent evaluations for all required objective control tests. Verification of the instrumentation by using external measuring equipment should be repeated if major modifications and/or repairs are made to the control loading system. Note 2: FSTD static control testing (tests 2.1 and 2.2) from the second set of pilot controls is required only if both sets of controls are not mechanically interconnected on the FSTD. A rationale is required from the data provider if a single set of data is applicable to both sides. If controls are mechanically interconnected in the FSTD, a single set of tests is sufficient. Dynamics testing is not required at both pilot positions. Note 3: For the control sweep tests (tests 2.a.1, 2.a.2 and 2.a.3), in order to enable validation of steep force gradients near control stops, an additional tolerance of ± 1.5% of total travel on the position axis should be applied. Procedure: perform a running take-off or a running landing and note a change (increase or decrease) with speed in fuselage vibrations (as opposed to rotor vibrations) due to the friction of dragging the skid along the surface. This vibration will lessen as the ground speed decreases. X X 13.2 Translational lift effect (including transverse flow effect). Procedure: from a stabilized in-ground-effect (IGE) hover, begin a forward acceleration. When passing through the effective translational lift range, the noticeable effect will be a possible nose pitch-up in some helicopters, an increase in the rate of climb, and a temporary increase in vibration level (in some cases this vibration may be pronounced). This effect is experienced again upon deceleration through the appropriate speed range. During deceleration, the pitch and rate of climb will have the reverse effect, but there will be a similar, temporary increase in vibration level. X X

Chapter 7 – E valuation Crit eria and Requirements for Additional Qualifications Page 7-1 Chapter 7 - Evaluation Criteria and Requirements for Additional Qualifications 7.1 Overview (1) The qualifications described in this Chapter may be mandatory or optional for some qualification levels (as prescribed in Chapters 4 and 5 Qualification Performance Standards (QPS)), or can be included as an additional qualification for other Flight Simulator Training Devices (FSTD) levels that are modified to meet the requirements herein. This appendices in this chapter describe the FSTD evaluation criteria and requirements, regardless of the level, that the National Simulator Evaluation Program (NSEP) will use to qualify an FSTD for pilot training and checking in the following special manoeuvers: (a) Windshear Training Program Use; (b) Full Stall Training Tasks; (c) Upset Prevention and Recovery Training Tasks; (d) Engine and Airframe Icing Training Tasks; (e) Takeoff and Landing in Gusting Crosswinds; and (f) Bounced Landing Recovery Training Tasks. (2) To qualify an FSTD for the additional qualification in this chapter, the sponsor must make their request in the letter of intent for an initial evaluation, or subsequently in accordance with the procedure at section 3.7 of Chapter 3. (3) Additional qualifications not presented in this chapter may also be eligible for evaluation provided that the sponsor confirms with the Training Program Approval Authority (TPAA) prior to the evaluation that the intended training and checking is relevant to the approved training program. (4) In cases where this manual does not address the evaluation criteria and requirements for unique or special qualifications, the sponsor should consult with the Manager Simulator Program (MSP) to determine what evaluation criteria will be used and whether any addition data are required. 7.2 Aeroplane Full Flight Simulator - Qualification Requirements for Windshear Training Program Use (1) Applicability. This section applies to all simulators, regardless of qualification level, that are used to satisfy the training requirements of any Transport Canada-approved training program that addresses windshear encounters. (2) Statement of Compliance and Capability. (a) The sponsor must submit a Compliance and Capability (SOC) confirming that the aerodynamic model is based on flight test data supplied by the airplane manufacturer or other approved data provider. The SOC must also confirm that any change to environmental wind parameters, including variances in those parameters for windshear conditions, once inserted for computation, result in the correct simulated performance. This statement must also include examples of environmental wind parameters currently evaluated in the simulator (such as crosswind takeoffs, crosswind approaches, and crosswind landings). (b) For simulators without windshear warning, caution, or guidance hardware in the original equipment, the SOC must also state that the simulation of the added hardware and/or software, including associated flight deck displays and annunciations, replicates the system(s) installed in the airplane. The statement must be accompanied by a block diagram depicting the input and output signal flow, and comparing the signal flow to the equipment installed in the airplane. (3) Models. The windshear models installed in the simulator software used for the qualification evaluation must do the following:

Chapter 7 – E valuation Crit eria and Requirements for Additional Qualifications Page 7-2 (a) Provide cues necessary for recognizing windshear onset and potential performance degradation requiring a pilot to initiate recovery procedures. The cues must include all of the following, as appropriate for the portion of the flight envelope: (i) Rapid airspeed change of at least ±15 knots (kts). (ii) Stagnation of airspeed during the takeoff roll. (iii) Rapid vertical speed change of at least ±500 feet per minute (fpm). (iv) Rapid pitch change of at least ±5º. (b) Be adjustable in intensity (or other parameter to achieve an intensity effect) to at least two (2) levels so that upon encountering the windshear the pilot may identify its presence and apply the recommended procedures for escape from such a windshear. (i) If the intensity is lesser, the performance capability of the simulated airplane in the windshear permits the pilot to maintain a satisfactory flightpath; and (ii) If the intensity is greater, the performance capability of the simulated airplane in the windshear does not permit the pilot to maintain a satisfactory flightpath (crash). Note: The means used to accomplish the "non-survivable" scenario of paragraph 3.b.(2) of this section, that involve operational elements of the simulated airplane, must reflect the dispatch limitations of the airplane. (c) Be available for use in an approved windshear flight training program. (4) Demonstrations. (a) The sponsor must identify one survivable takeoff windshear training model and one survivable approach windshear training model. The wind components of the survivable models must be presented in graphical format so that all components of the windshear are shown, including initiation point, variance in magnitude, and time or distance correlations. The simulator must be operated at the same gross weight, airplane configuration, and initial airspeed during the takeoff demonstration (through calm air and through the first selected survivable windshear), and at the same gross weight, airplane configuration, and initial airspeed during the approach demonstration (through calm air and through the second selected survivable windshear). (b) In each of these four situations, at an "initiation point" (i.e., where windshear onset is or should be recognized), the recommended procedures for windshear recovery are applied and the results are recorded as specified in paragraph 6.2.5 of this section. (c) These recordings are made without inserting programmed random turbulence. Turbulence that results from the windshear model is to be expected, and no attempt may be made to neutralize turbulence from this source. (d) The definition of the models and the results of the demonstrations of all four (4) cases described in paragraph 4.a. of this section, must be made a part of the Master Qualification Test Guide (MQTG). (5) Recording Parameters. (a) In each of the four MQTG cases, an electronic recording (time history) must be made of the following parameters: (i) Indicated or calibrated airspeed. (ii) Indicated vertical speed. (iii) Pitch attitude. (iv) Indicated or radio altitude. (v) Angle of attack. (vi) Elevator position.

Chapter 7 – E valuation Crit eria and Requirements for Additional Qualifications Page 7-3 (vii) Engine data (thrust, N1, or throttle position). (viii) Wind magnitudes (simple windshear model assumed). (b) These recordings must be initiated at least 10 seconds prior to the initiation point, and continued until recovery is complete or ground contact is made. (6) Equipment Installation and Operation. All windshear warning, caution, or guidance hardware installed in the simulator must operate as it operates in the airplane. For example, if a rapidly changing wind speed and/or direction would have caused a windshear warning in the airplane, the simulator must respond equivalently without instructor/evaluator intervention. (7) Qualification Test Guide. (a) All Qualification Test Guide (QTG) material must be forwarded to the MSP. (b) A simulator windshear evaluation will be scheduled in accordance with normal procedures. Continuing qualification evaluation schedules will be used to the maximum extent possible. (c) During the on-site evaluation, the evaluator will ask the operator to run the performance tests and record the results. The results of these on-site tests will be compared to those results previously approved and placed in the QTG or MQTG, as appropriate. (d) QTGs for new (or MQTGs for upgraded) simulators must contain or reference the information described in paragraphs 6.2.2, 6.2.3, 6.2.4, and 6.2.5. (8) Subjective Evaluation . The NSPM will fly the simulator in at least two of the available windshear scenarios to subjectively evaluate simulator performance as it encounters the programmed windshear conditions. (a) One scenario will include parameters that enable the pilot to maintain a satisfactory flightpath. (b) One scenario will include parameters that will not enable the pilot to maintain a satisfactory flightpath (crash). (c) Other scenarios may be examined at the MSP’s discretion. (9) Qualification Basis. The addition of windshear programming to a simulator in order to comply with the qualification for required windshear training does not change the original qualification basis of the simulator.
